utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This Status Conference will shade imperceptibly I hope into the trial. We will sit first session until 9.35, a 30-minute break; then 10.05 until 11.40, another 30-minute break; and then 12.10 until 1.45. This conference has come about as a result of something that happened, an exchange between Mr. Milosevic and myself some weeks ago. We were looking at the progress of the Defence case, and I remarked then to Mr. Milosevic that continuing at this same pace at the end of 150 days he would have had no more than 100 or 120 witnesses. Mr. Milosevic then commented to the effect that that only served to illustrate how unreal and unfair the entire system and entire allocation of time was in relation to him. I was, naturally, very concerned about that, bearing in mind that the Prosecution called about 300 witnesses. So I caused an inquiry to be made into the number of written statements utilised by the Prosecution in the presentation of their case, and the result of that inquiry is in a document that was circulated yesterday to all parties. It shows, Mr. Milosevic, that for the Croatia indictment, there were slightly more written statements than live testimony. And for the Bosnia indictment more than twice as many written statements as live testimony. And the Kosovo indictment, written statements exceeded live testimony by almost two-thirds. And looking at the three indictments as a whole, you will see the figures on the second page. Total number of Prosecution witnesses, 352. Total number of live witnesses 114. Which means that only about a third of the witnesses testified live. The rest, two-thirds, gave testimony by way of written statements. And then, of course, added to that is the fact that a number of these witnesses had their statements admitted without cross-examination, some 15 per cent. So that would explain why at the end of the 150 days assigned Mr. Milosevic might not have adduced evidence from more than 100, 120, 130 witnesses. It means, therefore, Mr. Milosevic, that you have to take account of what is open and available to you through the Rules by way of written statements, 92 bis, 89(F), and the other facilities that are open. I should say that as far as 92 bis and 89(F) are concerned, those matters are not entirely unrelated to some of the issues which are outstanding for consideration by the Trial Chamber as evidential questions raised by the -- by the Prosecution. The Status Conference, of course, will be open to the parties to submit other points, but we don't want to -- to stray too far, and we have a limited time, and I thank the Prosecution for the notes which they submitted on the 13th. I want first, though, to hear from the parties in relation to the opening remarks that I made in relation to the use of written statements by the Defence and the impact that that might have on the progression of the trial. I'll hear first from Mr. Milosevic, then Mr. Kay, then Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, any comments on the opening remarks? Or if you prefer to speak last, you can have the benefit of speaking last. It's a benefit in some -- in a particular sense. We're not hearing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume if I say something now I can also say something later on, if I have something to say. And you indicated quite rightly, Mr. Robinson, in commenting on these figures, the figures that you presented in this internal memorandum, with the proviso that I should like to draw your attention to some other aspects of that interpretation. In the total, as you yourself said, only one-third of the witnesses testified live, viva voce. I think that that goes to the detriment of the principle of the public nature of the trial and greatly so. I assume that Mr. Nice can respond to that by saying that all the documents are accessible to the public, of course, and that they can be placed at their disposal or, rather, that they are at their disposal being produced on the Internet and so on. However, the general public doesn't use that type of information, and it is only what is going on here live and what is stated here viva voce can truly be considered to be public and open to the public. So that you know my position full well. I would like witnesses who testify here to testify publicly. And second, even this one-third of witnesses, we would have to look at how many of them testified in fact in closed session of the people testifying viva voce, and based on an agreement with the Prosecution. So that that percentage, if taken that percentage into consideration, the overall percentage would be lower. I think that this is a very vital question of principle, and I don't think that we should look at it simplistically. As far as the overall time is concerned, total time, you quite rightly presented my view, that is to say, that this just illustrates how little time I was given in the first place for all three large indictments, that is say, Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, the extensive indictments. And I'd also like to draw your attention to the fact that parallel to calling witnesses I have to see and interview the witness beforehand, and the time for that is far shorter, incomparably shorter, in fact, than Mr. Nice has for his witnesses, Mr. Nice and his associates, of course. And this boils down to one meeting and a fairly short one at that and completely inadequate time for preparation. So this is very short time on all counts. And of course you can expect that I shall be asking for a prolongation of that time, extension of the deadline. Now, with respect to the bill [In English] Use of time [Interpretation] mathematics provided by the Registry, I have nothing to say on that score. I assume that the people who have counted up the time are very responsible individuals and are keeping records responsibly. However, I should like to draw your attention to one aspect of this matter. In your decision, in your ruling, you said that with respect to the time that I myself have for the examination-in-chief the opposite side has 60 per cent of that time, of the time I use, for their cross-examination, which would mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm trying not to get into that particular question today, and in fact the Prosecutor had been disposed to discuss that particular question, and we made a decision to the contrary. So let's not get into that question. We'll deal with that on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just wanted to draw your attention to the fact that if for every ten hours that I have, the other side has six hours. And if you compare the figures, then you'll see that the balance has been upset. I expect you to do a minimum, and that is to look at my time in relation to the time used up by the other party so that we have the 10-to-6 ratio prevail as you yourself said. Otherwise, I am doing my best to use my time as rationally as possible, both in terms of preparation and in terms of my examination-in-chief and my questioning here, that it be useful so that you can see what actually happened and learn what actually happened. And I am bearing in mind the fact that we have accusations made here where everything has been turned topsy-turvy, upside down, or, rather, in which highly improbable things are being asserted. So it is quite justified for us to hear the witnesses, to hear the arguments put forward so we can gain an insight of everything that is going on. So that the time factor is not just a technical factor, technicality, it is a factor of essential importance and basic importance for asserting the elementary principle of truth. And in that respect, I expect you to have great understanding for the work in hand and the time it requires. So much from me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just considering the principal issue in terms of evidence when we're looking at the allocation of time. It is the written evidence, the oral testimony debate that really this centres upon. And during the course of the Prosecution case, the jurisprudence was changed at the Tribunal in relation to the use of Rule 92 bis and the development of Rule 89(F). On behalf of the Defence, it has to be said that the use of Rule 92 bis and its procedures are more suitable as a Prosecution vehicle for the adduction of evidence. I think it would be fair to submit that that was a development within the Rules largely for the benefit of the Prosecutor, and its emphasis as a tool for the Defence has not really been something that has been fully countenanced in the cases before the Tribunal. It's not been something that is available for the Defence, not been something that was envisaged the Defence would avail itself of to a great extent. And the submission on behalf of the accused comes down to this: That as he sees it, the issues are best on his behalf heard through viva voce evidence rather than the use of the technical rules for the introduction of evidence in a written form which may suit the progress of a case for the Prosecutor. As we're dealing with the narrow issue here, I put that before the Trial Chamber as a matter of consideration on the use of the Rules to, from his point of view, maximise what is available within this allotted period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you not consider, Mr. Kay, that a lot of the evidence that is being presented in this particular case by the Defence is eminently suitable for presentation in writing? Just take as an example the witness we have concluded. The bulk of his testimony in chief could have easily been presented in writing because it was factual, and it could have been supplemented by questions on issues that the accused was concerned to emphasise and then it could have been cross-examined within a reasonable scope and concluded in probably a third or certainly a half of the time in which it was concluded. And it's a type of evidence that I suspect is in this case rather different from the scenario that you're envisaging, where Defence evidence of criminal responsibility might have to be presented viva voce. I understand the point. But I think this way this case has developed or evolved that there is evidence of a nature very similar to the Prosecution evidence that you are categorising as suitable for these two Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a resource issue for the Defence in relation to getting people to provide written reports. And I had experience of that when dealing with matters the end of last year on the Racak incident itself, asking for a report that could have been used, perhaps, as written testimony, or going through the Rule 94 bis channel. You're faced with a demand of, well, pay me for 300 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand. Again, I understand that point. But my problem with that is that that's rather an academic issue because the will isn't there to even start that process at the moment. Mr. Milosevic is not interested in following that course, so we don't know realistically what the outcome would be. It's -- you are dealing with and he material different situation for a number of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I just flag that up, though, on this use by the Prosecution of the written methods of production of evidence against the Defence being able to. There is a resource issue and a time issue to get witnesses to undertake such projects. And in terms of supervision and work preparation to get a proper statement taken rather than an interview requires, and the Prosecution would no doubt acknowledge this, several people being involved in the process, facilities, resources to take a full and proper statement of 20 pages, say, as we've had from the Prosecution through various Rule 89(F) witnesses. It is difficult for Defence resources to often achieve what seems a very desirable and worthwhile way of producing evidence. There are practical problems that are faced. On the matter of the will, I can't deal with that, and I have to leave that to Your Honours. Those are my observations on this narrow issue at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, not very much that I need to say on this topic. The Chamber should in our respectful submission stick absolutely to its original time allocation and the accused should be reminded of that because of two things. First, the potential to use written evidence has been drawn to the accused's attention by the Prosecution and by the Court I think really from the beginning of his Defence case and various points throughout it. Second, the accused persists in misunderstanding the reason for and value of public trials that happen in this court under the expansive adversarial system, even if they would not have necessarily have happened in other countries. And the purpose of open and public trials is to allow public supervision of the judiciary and the executive where the executive is involved so that it can be seen that what they do is fair. It is not to provide entertainment. Still less is it to provide an opportunity for propaganda. Now, the accused is quite unashamed in saying that he's not speaking to you. He's speaking to a different audience. He's not indeed addressing matters necessarily forensically. He's addressing different matters through the medium of a public trial, the public nature of which is fully available. For example, the accused correctly says that I would say the material is all available to those seeking to inquire into it, and so it is. And indeed in the Defence case or indeed in the case as a whole there's been very little closed-session testimony, far less than any or most other cases here. And therefore, if he persists in presenting his case on a false premise as to the value, significance, or utility of the public nature of the trial, then he has own himself to blame for the fact that he will not be able to get as much evidence in in the allotted and reasonable time as he otherwise could. Turning to Mr. Kay's observations about the different utility of 92 bis or 89(F) for the Prosecution as opposed to the Defence. There may be some merit in that observation so far as 92 bis and what is referred to as crime base evidence. Not a phrase I've ever liked. Crimes, I suppose, is a better term. Where it could reasonably have been expected that the evidence would be unchallenged in whole or in part in the event that didn't turn out. But that argument says nothing about the general utility of 89(F) which can be used for absolutely any type of evidence, and indeed in our respectful submission should be. In my personal submission, should be in all cases and for nearly all evidence in all Prosecution and Defence in order to make the best use of the finite and limited resources of this Tribunal as a whole. So that there is absolutely no reason for the accused not to use 89(F) or 92 bis. Mr. Kay is of course correct that preparing written statements takes some time. Two points or three on that. First, and as a matter of fact, the Court has regularly enough -- I was going to use the word "court" but perhaps "detective" is a better neutral phrase, witnesses speaking from quite extensive notes and may have judged that to quite a significant degree the exchanges between the accused and the witnesses are -- follow a prepared format. Nothing wrong with that. But of course it's only a small step between prepared format with supporting notes and a disciplined written statement characteristically as the Chamber will recall from the Prosecution's side of about ten sides or less of fairly broadly spaced type. Second point: The accused is not in a position simply because he has elected to represent himself to pray that in aid on matters where he should be assisting the Chamber to the most efficient use of time. He has associates. He has Mr. Kay and Ms. Higgins there to assist him. It is well within his ability with his resources or with further resources that he can obtain and deploy to prepare written statements for all the witnesses that he seeks to call and to rely on the provisions of 89(F) which will of course impose a much greater burden on the Prosecution which will have to be cross-examining witnesses at a much more swift rate, one following the other. So those are two -- two points that I would draw to your attention. If he chooses not to rely on 89(F), then that is his choice with consequences that will be determined by him. Your Honours, I should also make this point, and it's one of the points I touch in on the notes for this Status Conference: The more particularised the advance notice given by a party to another party of evidence to come the more it should be possible for cross-examination to be both prepared and limited. Not only will it be possible from time to time to make concessions and thus to eliminate altogether at a first read of a document something from the list of issues facing the Trial Chamber, but it should be possible and I think usually is to make better use of time in cross-examination. And that, of course, is particularly important in relation to evidence that is of an expert nature although coming in in the guise of factual evidence and other problems which I refer in the notes provided in advance. I have nothing else, I think, to say on the narrow points raised Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, anything in reply? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I see nothing to which there is any need to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, on the notes that you produced, I'm not sure whether we have time to go into all of them, all of the points, but you might wish to highlight two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm much obliged. It may help if I summarise the Prosecution's position in this way: Is of course very concerned about the overall length of the trial timetable. Potentially as it stands even more so were there to be any question of prolongation, and its concerns are not just either particular to the staff members or to the resources of the Office of the Prosecutor but much broader than that. There are many reasons why this trial should be brought to a timely conclusion. With that in mind and with the assumption that we would invite the Chamber to say it is entitled to make that adequate resources will be made available to Office of the Prosecutor, to the assigned counsel and to the accused to meet any demands that the Trial Chamber makes of us as parties, we would press you to notify the accused and the rest of us immediately that steps to the conclusion of this trial will be seamless, that there will not be an expectation of or allowance for breaks between the end of the Defence case, rebuttal, rejoinder. I omitted to deal with Rule 98, but any Rule 98 witnesses, closing arguments, written and oral, that it is in everybody's interests, and it is a major interest that a timetable should be set and requirements should be made of all of us that this case proceeds without breaks to its conclusion. I have set out in the document which is an internal document but available of course to the parties particular mechanisms by which that should be done. The second point which I've touched on already is that the only interest, the only legitimate interest that this trial has is the forensic interest of getting a fair result. It's not a case where there is any legitimate interest in the accused having more publicity of the type he candidly acknowledges he seeks. And with that in mind, I've set out some specific proposals for how the closing stages of this trial should be dealt with in order to assist the Court and to serve no other purpose, and in particular, how the accused should be confined firmly both as to written submissions under I think it's Rule 95, is it, closing arguments -- sorry, Rule 86, and as to oral submissions, and I would press the Chamber to consider the wisdom of that and to make preliminary orders now so that the accused knows he has to prepare a written argument that will deal with the legal and factual issues on a count-by-count basis, to assist the Chamber and to allow for responsive arguments from ourselves or assisting arguments from the assigned counsel if their involvement is requested. Similarly, the issue of the accused giving evidence or making an unsworn statement should in our respectful submission be confronted immediately for the following reason -- two reasons: One, the accused is already in default in respect of an order that he should announce whether he's on his own witness list. Two, if he is going to make an unsworn statement or give evidence, that will take some time. Time should be allotted to it, then deducted from the 150 days, and that will then put the Chamber in a better position to supervise as it can his use of the time dividing it between the three indictments. And so we would invite the Chamber to deal with that as soon as may be or immediately to avoid the risk that the accused will simply push the Trial Chamber into a corner where it is obliged to give him more time, which is probably his sole interest at the moment apart from getting the evidence before you. One suspects that his underlying objective will be to get more time to make this trial last even longer than it's lasted already. The third point I deal with at paragraph 15. This trial is proceeding at the pace of just over 12 hours of court sittings a week. By any international standards, that is of course a very short sitting per week. The accused's health was the reason for coming down to this low level of sitting. His health appears to have been robust but for a viral infection. We know the history of his health record and of the issues that led to the imposition of counsel, I think, and may have led to his now following the medical regime rather more precisely. There is every reason for the Chamber to reconsider the number of days sitting. And before the accused responds to that in a predictable way, let me make the Prosecution's position quite clear. If the accused is able to sit five days a week, the fact that he chooses to represent himself is no reason for sitting any less. The interests of the Court, the institution as a whole, and the general public are in having this -- having this case determined in a timely way, and if he is now fit to sit either five or four days a week, then the Court can and in our respectful submission should proceed on the basis that he has the resources available to him should he wish to use them to enable that period of time to be used in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a matter that I raised some weeks ago and indicated that we had it under active consideration. I indicated that we were considering inquiring of the doctors whether the accused would be able to work one day more per week for perhaps three of the four weeks in a month. We do have it under active consideration, as I said, and we will make a decision on that issue soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful and pleased to hear that on behalf of the Prosecution. Perhaps I should flesh out in one sentence one other technical point arising from the possibility of rebuttal and rejoinder cases and our concern about it, and our concern that there should be - I've touched on it already - no interval between the close of one part of the case and the start of the next. It should all be seamless with no gaps of any kind. And although I can think of no phrase I would personally more enjoy delivering or no sentence than the sentence there is no application to call rebuttal evidence and I am ready to make my closing argument, it is but least probable that I won't be in a position to deliver that sentence. With that in mind, and given that the accused is under an obligation to present his evidence indictment by indictment, I would invite the Chamber to allow or encourage the presentation of filings on possible rebuttal witnesses periodically through the balance of the accused's case, perhaps most conveniently one after the close of his Kosovo evidence and one after the close of his Croatia evidence, in order to either rule on them before the close of the Defence case or at least to make some provisional decisions or to communicate some provisional decisions so that preparations can be made in order that there could be no argument that time would be required between the close of case and calling of rebuttal evidence, if any, once the final decision is made as to what rebuttal evidence, if any, might be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have anything more to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of issues. Can I tell the Court, because looking at point 7 of the Prosecution's submissions, assigned counsel not to address facts in closing arguments, we think that that would be very wrong and unfair if such a provision was to go through. We're in fact currently working on a response to the Prosecution fill-box, and so we're going through the evidence from the beginning and putting in an extra column onto their fill-box and responding to the arguments that they have put in there on evidential matters. It has to be done, and we believe it's a very valuable guidance for us to do for the Trial Chamber is as you go through it, and you'll see -- it's not a criticism of Mr. Nice, but there are vast passages of text that are replicated throughout, applied to counts and allegations, some of which bear actual -- actually no relevance to the evidence that was heard, and we feel the Trial Chamber would be led into error if it followed the Prosecution arguments without any other party putting in a counterweight. On matters of law, we propose to put in a brief at the end of this on the legal issues so that we address the facts within the fill-box and put in a legal document containing legal argument as a separate vehicle. We've had several attempts over the last two months in finding a way of dealing with everything, and as we started one way we looked at an unwieldy document. We then went back to the drawing board and started again, and that's the approach we found most helpful, we believe, having been through various prototypes on the way to where we are now. And we've done it early because we realised that it would take time to work out the best shape. So we feel that that would be essential for the Trial Chamber. Whether the accused puts in his own written argument or addresses the Court orally on matters of law and fact, that it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That is certainly the view which the Chamber takes. And in fact, I was considering issuing an order requiring the assigned counsel to prepare such a brief. We would definitely be helped by a brief from the assigned counsel on the legal issues which, of course, can't be separated from the evidence, from the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I would rather hope that as the trial progresses assigned counsel would be taking notes of important issues that arise, some of which I have highlighted and which are in the interests of the accused, to raise points in that brief which the accused may miss himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because assigned counsel, from the experience which they have, may have a sharper eye for that kind of detail. So most certainly we will be expecting a legal brief from assigned counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can say in fact we started this project in December. As I said, it took awhile to get the right shape because it's big, the subject we're dealing with, and we looked to providing narrative, and none of that really worked, we felt, and so we've gone into the fill-box area. So it's under way, and the Court will have a concluded document at the end. How much time there is between the close of evidence and the submission of final briefs will be another matter. I think that that's best -- best addressed nearer to the -- when we're looking at the rebuttal evidence so that we have a timetable for that, then, and a more realistic hold on the overall evidence. We're also including within it as we progress issues, submissions on the evidence you're hearing from Defence witnesses and how that counters various Prosecution witnesses so that the Court has a map, if you like, of the issues from each witness, on a paragraph and count basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So those are the matters that I raise. I don't know whether the Trial Chamber wanted to hear on additional matters, whether they wanted assigned counsel to submit any evidence independently. We've been discussing this matter between ourselves on whether there would be an expectation. We haven't developed anything or put anything before the Court to date, but it's been at the back of our mind. As yet we don't know the full extent of the Defence evidence, but we were looking at issues such as the use of 92 bis by us using transcript evidence from other trials at the Tribunal, if there was helpful Defence expert evidence. And we've again in December or -- no, before then, started reviewing experts in other cases that the Defence have called and whether we would independently put that in to assist the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you might want to submit a filing on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If that's helpful to do so. Again, it's one of the issues we've been turning over as to where we go in relation to some of the evidence and issues in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, are you in a position to assist at all in point 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I know the associate for the accused, Professor Rakic, has been dealing with this issue. He hasn't actually been here since the end of last year. This is under way. I've actually made a draft and have this under hand first of all for the Americans. It may well be that something is being issued next week for the US embassy as well as directly to the witnesses themselves, and I have worked on that in relation to Albright and Clinton. In relation to the UK witnesses, I have in fact met the legal advisor yesterday and to open up channels there. So this is an area I have gone into, appreciating the issues concerning the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It should, of course, be addressed as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because we wouldn't want to have an application, say a week before the end of the time allocated for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: An application to deal with these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm trying to be as conclusive and consult as widely as possible on number 12, and I actually started from my end at the end of last year, and as a result of things a few weeks ago decided to just get on with it myself and do research on the issues and to try and meet as much as possible observations that I had received from the US legal advisor Mr. Kay when I met him at the end of last year. So that -- that I hope will in respect of two of the concerned countries, those internationals, something that's concluded in fact within three or four weeks, and then look at the other outstanding internationals from Germany and France. There may be a few other UN figures within it, but it's under -- under review now. So it's not being left to the end. I've started on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, first in relation to what Mr. Kay was speaking about now or, rather, in relation to the question that you put, I wish to remind you that in the month of February last year, through the liaison officer I provided a list of these witnesses. This is called the list of hostile witnesses starting with Clinton and all the others are there. So it's been 13 months now. Shortly after that, the liaison officer sent these letters to the respective embassies. The results and the replies have not been here yet. I drew your attention to that a few months ago. So there is no delay in relation to that that can be linked to any activity of mine. I acted in good time. Even before my half-time started I dealt with this matter. So please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, I can't allow you to make a comment of that kind without a response on behalf of the Chamber. It is true you have raised that issue several times, but on each and every occasion that you have raised it, it has been pointed out that you have not followed the required procedural requirements. And as a matter of fact, the last time you raised it I told you that if you insisted on raising it without meeting the procedural requirements, I would dismiss the application, and I did so orally without prejudice to your right to resubmit a proper application meeting all the requirements. You're being assisted in this regard now by -- by Mr. Kay, and we expect to have an application in proper form. And once that application is made, the Chamber will give it all the consideration that it deserves. It doesn't matter who the person is. If the requirements are met, the Chamber will issue a subpoena for that person. You're being assisted now, and we expect to have a proper application in as soon as possible. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, as far as I can remember, precisely then when I spoke about it last time, that was a few months ago, I heard that Mr. Kay informed you here that he was working on it. Now, as for what Mr. Nice suggested, I think that his suggestions are highly incorrect. His suggestion is to work without any breaks whatsoever. He claims, and I wrote that down here, that the aim of this accused is to make this last as long as possible. I think that with any common sense, no one could draw that kind of conclusion, that anyone can have that kind of intention of dragging things out. My aim is to present the truth, and that requires time. That is not identical to any other kind of aim of having this extended for as long as possible. That is nonsense. Finally, as for this proposal of Mr. Nice's to increase the number of days here to over three days a week, I wish to remind you of the fact that you adopted that proposal on the basis of the request put forth by the doctors a few years ago. Since that had not been observed, you brought me to a situation in which I had deteriorated health problems which were then of a greater length than would otherwise have been expected. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So if -- since we are talking about chronic cardiovascular problems here, during this year if my health has improved then this place should be advertised as a kind of spa for treating such problems. If you read what the doctors wrote about my health condition which was not any kind of excess. This was a lasting problem. It was quite clear that there could not have been any kind of improvement. Perhaps there only could have been a stagnation once it was ruled that we would be working three case a week. On the contrary. I have a request that is quite the opposite, to have longer breaks. Otherwise, you will not give me any opportunity of getting any rest whatsoever. Even today under these conditions I can get some fresh air only on Saturdays and Sundays, because objectively speaking, during the week I have only those two days left to talk to witnesses, those two days when we do not work here. So it's only Saturdays and Sundays that I can get some fresh air. The conditions are, therefore, highly unfavourable. That is why I believe and assert that this kind of proposal made by Mr. Nice is ill-intentioned. There is another thing I wish to say. As for the list of hostile witnesses, I'm going to give it some more thought. But I think I will take Rudolf Scharping, the former minister of defence of Germany from that list, because in the meantime he made a statement to the effect that he had been manipulated. So it's not necessary really to establish who it was who manipulated him. It is those who should be held responsible for his manipulation that should deal with that matter. So I will probably get him off that list, and this will be my contribution to decreasing the number of persons on the said list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I make a couple of points relating to what my learned friend Mr. Kay said about the fill-box document and about factual submissions. First, as the Chamber may recall, we are reformatting the fill-box document into the standard computer system that is operated by the OTP. Indeed it may be possible at some stage to offer to the Chamber, to the accused and indeed of course to Mr. Kay instruction in how that system, if it comes in the computerised system, can be used to retrieve evidence by various criteria. I would, of course, be only too pleased to receive from Mr. Kay or Ms. Higgins corrections or observations they want to make about the document before it's submitted to the Chamber because there's no need for the Chamber to be burdened with shortcomings that are not significant for final deliberation but that would otherwise be irritating, and I hope Mr. Kay or Ms. Higgins feel they could do that. They are I know finding the document helpful. Coming back from the details of that this: My observations about whether the assigned counsel should make factual arguments is one of principle. Once a person elects to present his case himself and find himself put in the driving seat to the extent that the accused has at his own request been put, then the factual case he argues is his case, and it may not be either right that there should be two factual arguments. It may not indeed be what he wants, and we've heard many occasions where he has diverged from arguments advanced by Mr. Kay. So on factual arguments, I would maintain the Prosecution's position that there is neither the need nor is it desirable that factual arguments should be advanced independently by Mr. Kay from those advanced by the accused. Of course if Mr. Kay prepares a factual argument, whether structured on the Prosecution's computerised recording of and scheduling of evidence and the accused says, "Yes, please, I'd like to present that as my argument," then all to the good because he takes the benefit of it and it would obviously go in. But if there are any freestanding factual arguments by the assigned counsel different from those advanced by the accused, the Chamber will be in the difficult position of knowing which case it is to respond to. Fundamentally, as I say, a person who elects to conduct his own case is bound by the consequences of that decision insofar as factual arguments are concerned. On the topic of internationals, I'm not quite clear from what we've been told whether my learned friends and the accused are working cooperatively together or separately. The assertion by the accused that he has sent letters requesting witnesses to at least two embassies is something that I may wish to return to, but I simply say I'm not in a position to know whether that's the case or not. Certain it is that the accused has been told on every conceivable occasion of the need to get on with these applications because of the time two of the governments concerned take to process them. As I've indicated, longer probably than already is left in his case between now and the end of the year. It would normally be longer than you would actually take to get these witnesses processed through two of the governments. And lastly: If by himself or by Mr. Kay or Ms. Higgins he is seeking to call internationals of one kind or another, then I would press the Court to take that into account into the supervision of his allocation of time between the three indictments in the same way as I pressed the point in relation to his giving of his own evidence. Because any of these witnesses may take a lot of time, and late application to call them, whether by neglect of court rules or otherwise, should not operate as a way of forcing the Chamber to extend the reasonable period of time that it has allowed the defendant, the accused, to present his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I did mention that and say that it would be unreasonable to make such an application a week or two before the end of the time period allocated. The Chamber would not accept that as a basis for prolonging the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm obliged, and I have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course the Chamber will be considering all these matters, and if it considers it appropriate will issue an order, but there are one or two matters which it might be useful to raise. If we are to extend the sitting days from three to four, we wouldn't do that without the benefit of advice from the doctors because, in the first place, we're sitting three days a week as a result of the advice of the doctors, and we wouldn't change that regime without having their views. But it was occurring to the Chamber, Mr. Kay and Mr. Nice, and Mr. Milosevic, that today we are sitting from 8.00 to 9.35, then 10.05 to 11.40 and then 12.10 to 1.45, whether that sitting period could not be considered as an alternative. We would end up with roughly three hours -- or two and a half hours per week more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that will not advance the hours that many of us come here in any event. So we can manage it; although I recognise the very considerable additional strain it would place on my immediate resource. But as I've already explained, if the Chamber makes demands it's up to the Office of the Prosecutor, the assigned counsel and the accused to find the resources that are available to them to meet those reasonable demands, and we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is something that we would consider without necessarily seeking the advice of the doctors. If we are going to sit for an additional day or longer per week, we would certainly have to have the advice of the doctors. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're here already by then anyway, so it doesn't make any inconvenience to us. So it's not a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's just an idea which has just occurred to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And there are a number of ramifications which would have to be considered. There is staffing and administrative implications which would have to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sometimes the half-hour break during the course of the day gives you, well, obviously more time than 20 minutes, but I mean to say you can get more done in little preparations and things, copying of documents, circulation of documents, reading of documents in that time, which can be quite helpful on the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, that's the fourth day, then, which you're going to add but in a different way, in a roundabout way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would not be as long as a day, Mr. Milosevic. It's just two and a half to three hours. A day is about four hours. Mr. Milosevic, there's one matter that I might raise with you. Mr. Nice mentioned the question of whether you would be giving evidence or making an unsworn statement, a matter addressed in our omnibus order of the 17th of June in which we said that the accused shall indicate whether he intends to give evidence, when he intends to do so, and how long he anticipates his evidence would take. No time frame was set within which you should make that indication, but I ask the question of you now: Whether you intend to give evidence and when and how long do you anticipate it would take.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, meaning you do not intend to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not intend to, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that mean, then, that you would make an unsworn statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already made two statements and made an opening address, opening statement. And I don't want to testify because I would have to take the solemn declaration before an institution which I consider to be illegal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you haven't answered the question whether you will make an unsworn statement. Do I take it that you will not make any statement at all then?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I have already made two statements here and made an opening statement as well. And I have the right for my closing statement as well as far as I'm able to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you do have a right to make a closing statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can just interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to say I don't take the observations of the accused as an answer to a very clear question. But that drives me to link this point with one of the little points I made in my agenda for today where I suggested that at the closing arguments stage the greatest assistance would be given by a dialogue between the Chamber and the parties following the presentation of written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought we had been past that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know, but -- that's what I suggested, that the parties would be obliged to answer questions. And I had that in mind when I come back to say that here the Chamber asked the accused a very direct question and he really declined to answer it. I would press the Chamber to get an answer from him because it impacts both on the timetable and will also drive him to recognise that the time may come if my arguments on the agenda are there where he will have to enter a dialogue with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the question you say wasn't answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure he's answered the question as whether he's going to make a closing unsworn statement. The first three answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He has given a very clear answer that he is neither going to give evidence nor seek to make any other statement than a closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And obviously closing arguments might lead to the Court having a hearing at which it wants further information from -- further submissions from the parties and that would be a matter for him at that stage to decide how he participated or didn't participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if the understanding is -- if the understanding is that his reference to his closing argument is under Rule 86, I have nothing further to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there are two matters I would wish to raise with you. On a rough calculation, as of today we are about one-third of the way through the 150 days. We're about 50 days now. And that's a very rough assessment based on the earlier calculations. Can you give some indication of how far you are from the end of the presentation of the Defence case in relation to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we just clarify one point, Mr. Bonomy? Looking at your paper for the purposes of this present Status Conference, I see on it that up until now I have used a little less than a quarter, and this is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 88, 360. So that would make it a little less than a quarter of my time. I have indicated when Mr. Robinson said that wasn't the topic of our discussion here today, I did say that with respect to your ruling that the ratio should be, as you said, that the opposite side would have the right to use 60 per cent of my time. So for all of my ten hours, 6 hours, the ratio of 10 to 6 and vice versa. For every six hours used by Mr. Nice, ten hours that I use. Ten of my hours. So as you can see, according to the arithmetic so far, without entering into the time you previously allotted, because the Prosecution in cross-examination says here 58 hours, 43 minutes, et cetera, et cetera. So let's say 60 hours. Let's bring it to a round figure. So with respect to their hours, I -- that should give me 100 hours already that I should have had 100 and not 88 because it is in the ratio of 10 to 6. That's the portion that you yourselves set. So in that respect I assume that you're going to make the right corrections using basic arithmetic at least. And I should like to say straight away here and now so that you don't say that I have overstepped my time that I am going to ask for more time, because without a doubt I will need more time in order to hear the relevant witnesses for the indictments of that been stipulated here. And that is in the interests of justice and fairness, and not in the interests of using up more time or prolonging the proceedings as Mr. Nice said, that that's what I was trying to do, to drag it out. Please believe me, I don't take any pleasure in prolong -- in my association here with Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder now if you'd be good enough to address the question I asked you, and that was if you could indicate how far you are from the end of the presentation of your case in relation to Kosovo. In other words, how many more hours do you think it will take to present that case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if I can add this: The statistics in relation to time used by you was taken as of 10th of March. I'm afraid you've passed one-third already by now. I'm not sure about the exact data.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take that on board, Mr. Kwon, absolutely, what you've just said. But I'm just using the statistics that I have available, the facts and figures available. I don't wish to make, to construe anything else and to do my own additions. But I realise there is a time lag between the time that the statistics were presented and the time that we hold our discussions here. But if you have the available statistics, then that's sufficient to have a discussion on this. Now, Mr. Bonomy, I can't answer you were question exactly as to how much more time I need for Kosovo. All I can tell you is this: That I had planned my timing and my schedule, and in doing so I thought that I would be using a little more than a third of my time for Kosovo, a little more, but not half my time which I have at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second matter that I wish to raise to you is in relation to point 14 of the document produced by the Prosecutor. We are conscious of your right to present your defence as you see fit, and we're also conscious of the fact that the preparation of very detailed 65 ter summaries would have been a considerable burden at the stage of the pre-Defence case stage. However, the tendency recently has been for you to produce fairly brief lists of witnesses. I'm not complaining about that. That -- because of the time the witnesses take creates for me no problem. It may create certain difficulties for the Prosecutor. But it did strike me that it might be possible for you to produce better summaries of -- of the evidence you intend to lead from these witnesses in these little lists that you give us on a weekly basis. For example, it's pretty useless to be told that a witness will give evidence about personal knowledge of events in Kosovo. And it would help us a great deal to know what he will be giving evidence about, but I'm almost certain that it would assist your presentation of your defence case if you were to identify in advance what these issues are. Indeed, I am quite certain that we would be able to give greater assistance in directing the attention of the witness to the really relevant issues in the case if we had a better summary in advance. Now, is there a possibility that you could amplify these summaries in a way that would be of assistance both to the Trial Chamber and to your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. own presentation of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, certainly there is, yes. And I have no reason, apart from the time constraints, for me not to do that. So I'll do my best to give more complete summaries, to amplify my summaries. Yes, because this is a rather scant description, and you're quite right when you say that it's not sufficient when you read that a witness will testify to his own personal knowledge about the situation in Kosovo. That doesn't tell you a great deal. I quite agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I will do my best. I shall endeavour to go about this in a better way or, rather, to give you more extensive summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And sorry, there was -- there was one other matter I did omit to remember initially. Point 13. For exactly the same reasons, Mr. Milosevic, in both your interests and ours, from the point of view of a proper assessment of the evidence, it would be helpful if you could identify now - I don't mean this minute; I mean fairly quickly, in the next few days - the expert witnesses, those who are properly classed as experts who will be called by you throughout the trial, so that we can make adequate arrangements for the production and consideration by the Prosecutor of the reports of these experts. Now, would you be able to produce an indication of the expert evidence that you are likely to lead without committing yourself finally but likely to lead in the course of the remainder of the trial so that we can try to develop a programme for the preparation of any necessary witness reports?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. Bonomy. And I'll do that through my liaison officer. Now, as far as the summaries are concerned to which you pointed, please bear in mind this: The Trial Chamber stopped working when the opposite side stated that they had finished, and that was a time when I was in bed. And I was given six weeks to provide you with a list of witnesses and evidence and exhibits, and that is why the summaries are as brief as they are. Now, I assume that there are better conditions for the summaries to be written in a more useful way for you and for the list of witnesses, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope I made it clear to you that I understood that there were good reasons why these -- these summaries came in the form they did initially, and I'm grateful to you for considering improving the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe we are at the end of the Status Conference, and we will take a break now for 30 minutes and resume with the trial at 10.00. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I was trying to remember were you on your feet on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice had finished and I was to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it was -- I won't take long doing it as I made my primary submissions yesterday, but it's as a result of the questions of -- or comments by His Honour Judge Bonomy concerning the fairness of it as to what is happening with this witness. Since those observations by His Honour, we have been able to read the transcript of the proceedings in which Jasovic has given evidence in the other trial, the Limaj trial, and it is clear that the Prosecution are calling him as a witness of truth. They did not challenge his account of the matters and were putting him forward to the Tribunal as a witness upon whom the Court could rely. Within this courtroom, it is the intent of the Prosecution not to approach the witness in the same way. The Prosecutor is an indivisible organ. That's why it's called the Office of the Prosecutor. And in my submission it is unfair to the accused, and I'm drawing on the fairness that is within the articles within the Statute of the Tribunal for the Prosecution merely because the accused is calling or seeking to call this witness to then adopt a contrary point of view having called him as a witness in another case. That is unfair to this accused. And it's simply done on the basis that because an investigator or Mr. Saxon went to see the three witnesses over the weekend and took statements in which they denied that the content of their statements was true and they made allegations of forgery or oppression against this witness that the simple word of that witness has been taken. There has been no investigation by the OTP on this matter. It has gone no further than the assertions of those witnesses. And it was clear to call of us in relation to the deponent who said that his signature had been forged and he hadn't signed it that it seemed certainly at first blush looking at it that it was the same handwriting and that it may well not have been a truthful assertion, but none of those issues have in fact been investigated by Mr. Nice and the Prosecutor. They've just gone into further than saying, Mr. Milosevic wants to call this witness, it's on this basis, we oppose. We don't. We're not prepared to accept anything that he calls on his behalf without even looking into it, or even interviewing Mr. Jasovic about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are the issues in Limaj in relation to which the witness testified the same as the issues in relation to which he would testify here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's about his knowledge of people who were members of the KLA and his investigations as a police officer in the Orahovac area, Stimlje area. So it's his conduct as a police officer, and he's being called on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I don't think I suggested it was an issue of fairness. I was asking whether it was appropriate for this to happen, and that means, I think, that if it's an issue at all, it's not an issue necessarily of admissibility. Indeed it may be a situation in which the evidence has to be led for aught yet seen, but I still have this idea in my mind that the Prosecutor has to take a stand at some point one way or another. It may not be now. It may have to be later, once the evidence -- or the witness's evidence has been explored in two proceedings. At that stage he can't, as I see it, have it both ways. You can't imagine, for example, in a domestic jurisdiction. I see no difference here. A situation here where a police officer is charged with serious crimes against honesty or against the administration of justice and the prosecutor in that country presents that man as a truthful witness in another trial. I just can't envisage that situation occurring when he is the subject of allegations of perverting the course of justice and dishonesty. However, it may be that these have to be explored more fully before that decision is taken. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed Your Honour's word "appropriate" and so I then thought, well, how do we fit this into the jurisprudence when there are no guidelines which is why I went to the articles and to me it then became, if I was writing a text, a fairness issue where I was placing this that it's unfair. And we all know in domestic jurisdictions where cases have been overturned or stopped because there's been a contrary position concerning a police officer in one trial and his evidence in another. And it does seem that the Prosecution are prepared to shoot from the hip on an issue concerning this accused, Mr. Milosevic, and make assertions without investigating them. We all saw the handwriting of the statement. It was mentioned why don't you get a handwriting expert. But none of those investigations were pursued to get to the bottom of him as a witness. And he has been called in that trial as a witness of truth. So on those issues may -- may I make those points before the Court in addition to the ones I made yesterday, which I won't repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I -- sorry, if the accused is going to contribute, there's one matter of correction that I'd like to make at some stage and perhaps later would be better if the accused is going to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, without going into all of these procedural matters, I would like to remind you of something that is undoubtedly evident. When it comes to this witness, you had an opportunity to acquaint yourself with many facts concerning the terrorist activity in 1998 and 1999. This terrorist activity, the killing of people, ambushes, abductions of Serbs, Albanians, killing of policemen, troops, both Serbs and the Albanians, all of this has been discussed and presented here at length. Now let us see who are we dealing with here. Jasovic is a police inspector who based on the documents I placed in this binder that I wish to tender into evidence collected, gathered facts at a time when the community or the state was dealing with terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija. Therefore, at that time he collected facts on the terrorist activity in Kosovo and Metohija in order to identify members of the Kosovo Liberation Army which publicly announced its terrorist acts. He did that in order to identify the members of this organisation so that the police could arrest them and have them face the justice. I'm now putting a very simple question to you: Is there a single police force in the world which in the course of identifying members of a terrorist organisation collects false or wrong information that can be of no use in order to reach or to locate these members of terrorist organisations? He interviewed many individuals, and based on these interviews, many details emerged about individuals who were members of the terrorist organisation in an area where this inspector worked. He was an inspector in the Secretariat of the Interior of Urosevac which covers the municipalities of Stimlje, Racak, Petrovo Selo, Malopoljce, meaning the precise area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there are examples the world over of police forces fabricating cases against terrorists. It's an important area of miscarriage of justice in some of the most renowned systems in the world.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, you have to have something else in mind. This is an attempt by police to reach, to locate these terrorists. How is the police going to reach these terrorists if it is using wrong information? The particular people that the police interviewed, most of them were not even indicted or arrested. No. They were simply interviewed in order to gain information. And then the policemen would draft a note based on that, and this document would be given to somebody to sign it. There were always two police officers drafting or writing these notes. Since all of these official notes have been translated, you will see for yourself that they contain a large number of facts, that many facts can be identified and cross-checked from various sources based on the fact that a lot of other people had been interviewed. In addition to that, I would like to stress that all of this activity took place in 1998 and 1999. Therefore, it has nothing to do with any potential witnesses in this case or with the -- with Rule 92 bis. These are the documents which were created in the course of duties of police officer who in his attempt to collect as many facts as possible about the terrorist organisation and the perpetrators of the most grave crimes created these notes precisely in order to identify, locate, and arrest these perpetrators. Therefore, this involves a whole series of activities which were undertaken in order to apply the law and to act in accordance with the law in the course of police activities aimed at locating and apprehending these people. Therefore, there are a large number of interviews here. I even drafted a table, rather not I myself but my associates who went over these statements, and concluded, for example, that out of 40 persons who were killed in Racak and who were identified, 30 of them are mentioned in the statements of the persons interviewed as members of the KLA. One person is mentioned in as many of nine statements of various persons. Some of them are mentioned in fewer statements. Some are mentioned in five, in four, in three, most often in three or two statements, and there are some that are mentioned in four and in nine statements. Therefore, one can see very clearly that this is very relevant information which sheds light on a very important aspect of trying to establish what exactly happened in Racak. Gentlemen, you have to bear in mind that I have been accused by the opposite side for murder of these 40 people in Racak, and I maintain that none of the policemen who participated in the activities in Racak ought to be accused of murder because this was a police action. Shukri Buja who was a commander there explained to you that at a time when the police was entering Racak it was exposed to a very heavy machine-gun fire started by precisely members of the KLA. Therefore, you can see that it was a very grave conflict. And here in these documents, you can see that in Racak itself, in Petrovo, in Rance and in surrounding villages there was a very wide presence of the KLA which was very active. This is precisely -- these are precisely the issues covered by this police officer in his work. In addition to that, based on the interview I had with him, you will be able to see that in Urosevac where he served as a police officer in the SUP there, there were several police inspectors who were Albanians. They performed the same duties. Some of them later on perished after our forces withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija. You will see that even now this inspector maintains contacts with Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija from his current place of work. He continues to maintain contacts. Therefore, it is completely logical to have this witness heard here. In addition to that, Mr. Nice said, and I noted this down, that in this trial it became apparent that are reasons to doubt Jasovic's claims. I'm not sure that it became clear. I did not see it clearly for myself. What I saw is that Mr. Nice presented three statements here, three statements taken last week from three Albanians who claim that they had been forced and so on, that they had been under duress and so on. Gentlemen, let me tell you that there is not a single person who -- who lives today in Kosovo under the KLA terror and who will go on to admit that he or she had given some information to the police concerning the KLA activities. Not even the families of the KLA victims from that period of time dare testify about how their dearest and closest had been killed because they are afraid for their lives. Therefore, this is not a case where we have witnesses who could confirm what they had said, because then they gave a statement to the police of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think we have got the gist of your submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, one of the submissions that Mr. Kay made related to the evidence of a person commonly known as Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Exhibit 391. You said nothing on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've had a look at part of the transcript in relation to that, and while it seems confusing to say the least, it does appear that something in the order of 10.000 or more documents were introduced in the space of a moment or two in the course of his evidence. On a different interpretation they weren't introduced but I gather the general understanding is they were. Now, what have you to say about that? How does that differ from what's being proposed here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think these documents were introduced as a resource for consideration later going to show where particular people may have been at the time that they were engaged in combat. That was the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the difference between that and what's proposed to be done with the documents we're now considering?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, there is not a question of where individuals fell or were involved in combat. This is a much more focused issue as to whether particular people identified as victims were members of the KLA, they having been identified as victims in the indictment. So it's a much more focused issue, and it doesn't go to the generality that might be proved by a mass of evidence of individuals fighting in particular places under particular banners. So it's different to that extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have difficulty seeing this distinction. What's the difference between evidence that says these people are KLA fighters and evidence that says these people are Serbs who have fighting in Bosnia and Croatia? What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The two points I've made. One is it's a mass of evidence which would be beyond being called individually and is properly dealt with on this basis until challenged and disproved. And it goes to show not particular events. It goes to show the generality of where people were fighting. And turning it to the role of victims named in indictments whose particular status has to be proved not because, for example, the generality of people in the KLA operating in particular ways at this time might need to be established and indeed of course is conceded in the most general terms but for quite specific purposes related to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. particular counts in the indictment. So there are distinctions, significant distinctions. And where you've got a mass of evidence of the kind that's produced by Dragan that is beyond being dealt with individually, the Chamber is entitled to apply a different approach, bearing in mind that if the issue was ever challenged, either specifically or generally, the method of adduction of the evidence would be a matter of weight, and we have yet to see the degree to which, if any, that material is going to be challenged. Not material, the conclusions that we might invite to be drawn from that material which I think has hardly been considered in detail since. If it is challenged, then we'll have to wait to see what if any value there is in that material. But it may not be challenged because it may actually be that the accused's case on that point is not counter to the general effect of the evidence. It may be a matter of interpretation of the legal consequences of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, while I've read the evidence the case, I have to confess that these 10.000 or whatever pages have not been the subject of my scrutiny as yet. But can I take it from all you've said that there's no point here about these being documents which were prepared by someone whose interests or against whose interests they are now being used? There's not that distinction involved here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, no, I -- this particular witness produced them in an administrative way for other purposes as part of his so-called charity, I think, and simply to recall where people had been engaged. So there is no particular issue as to his having an interest to serve, that's true. Incidentally, Ms. Dicklich advises me that a representative sample was admitted as exhibits, but I don't think anything turns on that because it's the principle that Your Honour has in mind. I'm happy to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm unclear about what it was you have to say. But there are -- different interpretations might be made of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, to be specific, and I'm very grateful to Ms. Dicklich. The CD itself was marked for identification as 391 tab 1 and then tabs 2 to 8 of 391, a representative sample, were actually admitted. But, Your Honour, I'm don't -- I'm not going to -- that's just as a matter of detail. Your Honour's point which I must deal with remains of course for consideration. But apart from the factual differences, apart from the fact that we don't yet know to what extent, if any, there will be a real dispute between the parties over the underlying facts of these documents because it may actually be a matter of interpretation in law of what if anything flows from that that will be the defendant's -- or the accused's interests. There is this significant difference that here we are looking at identified individuals of manageable numbers identified as victims of particularised crimes. And, Your Honour, if I can turn to the couple of points I would wish to make arising from the things that the accused and Mr. Kay have said. It is now clear that the accused is relying on these records to show that some 30 of the victims were active members of the KLA. I haven't yet got through to finding 30 such names. I just tell you what the latest check if I'm able to -- Your Honour, just give me a minute. So far we've only identified, I think, one person clearly on the list who is named. There may be confusion as to other names arising from the multiple naming of -- or the different naming of individuals, and it's going to be a large exercise in analysis to find out first of all what these statements purport to say. Obviously Mr. Kay's table would be of assistance as would -- sorry, the accused's table would be of assistance if he wants to provide it. But at the moment we are not in a position to understand 30 named members of the KLA. But if there are as many as 30 named, then this is clearly something that the Prosecution has got to investigate, because for the same reason as I've said on several earlier occasions, if the investigation turns out to require some concession to be made by me then of course I'll make it and as soon as I possibly know that's my duty. And the arguments that are raised by both the accused and by Mr. Kay to which I'll turn simply highlight the need for the witnesses themselves to come and give evidence about what they knew of KLA membership. And I say that notwithstanding the accused's generalised assertion that no one in Kosovo at the moment is going to tell the truth about these things because that simply is an assertion he cannot realistically make, but I make it also because Mr. Kay's observation when he said it would be unfair for us to take a contrary view means that I'm basically obliged -- a point I made yesterday but I must emphasise, I'm basically obliged on his analysis to accept all these statements as gospel, simply because this witness has been called in another case, something I plainly cannot do. So they are all of these arguments this morning point yet again to the desirability on important matters or the necessity on important matters to go to the live witnesses first and not to consider hearsay or secondhand hearsay, all of which support the argument to exclude the evidence. But Your Honour, can I add just a couple more points. First of all, I quite understand Your Honour -- His Honour Judge Bonomy's concern about the possible need for a prosecution office ultimately to take a single view on a particular witness. Whether that applies in these cases is a matter that would in our submission require a little more careful consideration of all the circumstances, not least as exemplified arguably in this or these very cases because what may be said by witnesses about one side of events may be more likely to be acceptable than what they say about the other. So that I turn to this point, dealing with the examination, cross-examination, and re-examination of Jasovic in the other case. He was not being asked about the same topic as he's being invited to come and give evidence here.
