He was being invited in that case, as I understand it, to give evidence about the Serbs as victims essentially in a case which was charging Kosovo Albanians. So of course he in his position with his background, it may be argued, I'm not going to make this argument, but it might be argued would be more likely to be telling the truth about all that. Now, he was then cross-examined by counsel who had already raised arguments about the mistreatment of prisoners at the police station, again as I understand it. He was then cross-examined on the basis of the statements that we then obtained and had to be handed over and on the basis of other material going to show misbehaviour at this particular police station. And in re-examination, which I suspect would commend itself to this Chamber as a model, in re-examination the -- unless I've missed something, runs from page 5452 to 5453. He was asked four questions of a general nature, none of which I think can really be said as aimed at rehabilitating him on the particular point of the cross-examination about mistreatment. So that whether the Prosecution in that other case were taking a position specifically on the issues that would arise in this case is far from clear. Your Honour, when my learned friend says that we shoot from the hip, I really think that is a little bit of flourish that isn't justified. When this material was raised with us, what did we do? We went and inquired into it in the only way that was available to us at the time. We brought it back, handed it over to all the parties including as necessity to the other case as soon as we could and any other exercises that may be possible will be dealt with as soon as can be, but I'm not quite sure what else we could have done. And in this case, were this witness's evidence were allowed to be given in principle or at all over our objections, there would be a great deal of investigation to be done before I could responsibly take a position on the questions I should ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's assume for the moment, Mr. Nice, that the purpose of the evidence was to show how the system worked and that the product of the system led to the Judges being informed that there was significant KLA activity in and around Racak. Would you quibble with the evidence being used for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I doubt if I would because, after all, as the accused himself has explained to you, a witness we called explained the role of the KLA in Racak and indeed explained who fired the first shot on the morning in question. And as the Chamber realises from our indictment and opening and pre-trial brief, recognition --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. This is completely incorrect. This is quite incorrect. I mentioned Buja Shukri, the commander from the KLA from Racak who was a witness here, and he was the one who fired first in Racak. Not this witness. This witness was not in Racak at all. He's not testifying about that at all. Please bear in mind the fact that these are official documents of the relevant authorities about what they knew at the time concerned. And the direct link to this witness is the fact that he was the one who collected this knowledge and compiled official notes about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if we then take it just a stage further to test where we end up, where does the -- the issue about how these statements were obtained fit in? It may be said it doesn't matter. The authorities are getting this information and it doesn't matter whether they're getting it from policemen acting properly or improperly, or it may be said that somehow or other there is a link between this false information, allegedly false information coming in, the activity of the police officers who obtain it, and the criminal responsibility of the accused. Now, is there an issue of that sort surrounding the evidence of Jasovic if all he gave evidence about was the extent to which statements were obtained and submitted to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back two points. The accused completely misreads what I was explaining. I was explaining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you need to clarify that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The second thing is my position in answer to Your Honour's question was that I doubt if I would object to evidence coming from a witness like this given the generality of reported KLA activity, and that remains my position. I doubt if I would if it was restricted to that. I would of course have to check before I could completely waive it through that it was right to do so, and my means of checking it would be probably different in their intensity because of the comparatively less significance for the purposes of this case than the significance of evidence that goes to the heart of a particular indictment -- a particular count in the indictment. So, for example, to expand on Your Honour's question and my answer, if the evidence is adduced simply to show that, yes, there was extensive KLA activity in a particular region at a particular time and I happen to have the vaguest suspicion, guess, or even more that the evidence may have been obtained unsatisfactorily but nevertheless the evidence happens to be accurate, there's not a lot of point in my burdening the Chamber with any relevant issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What if it goes, though, to the point of saying that the Judges -- the authorities were informed that as many as 30 of the victims in Racak were reputed to have KLA links?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if that's what is going to be suggested was the effect of this witness's evidence, then I think a great deal more inquiry would be required of us, because if his integrity is open to doubt and having statements to suggest that he has obtained evidence improperly, is quite enough to raise the question of doubt. If there's evidence to show or material to show that his integrity should be doubted, then we are exploring or we would land up in a position of having to explore a police system that matches not at all the ideal standards to which we would all wish to aspire for our own countries and would mean quite inevitably that we would invite the Chamber not to accept at face value for purposes of the accused's state of mind the passage of information between one questionable organ and another within this overall system. We'd have to look at it a great deal more in detail. Now, in fact, the accused hasn't said in terms that that's the purpose I think for which he wants this information. He wants it to show that these people were KLA, which goes right to the heart of a count in an indictment. It was Mr. Kay who advanced in a slightly different formulation from Your Honour's, the possibility that it goes to the state of mind of the accused, but I can see Your Honour's formation as being significant, and correct me -- not correct me, I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, what Your Honour is suggesting is that if this information came however erroneous or however incorrectly elicited from deponents, it could justify an attack that would be criminal if it was better informed. I can see that as an argument. But I'm not in a position on -- to concede that it would be right for the evidence to go on that basis without a great deal more investigation. But, Your Honour, we would need it to be absolutely clear one way or another the purposes for which this evidence is being adduced, and here I repeat a phrase I've used earlier and on several occasions it's the accused's case. He wants this evidence to show that up to 20 people of those killed in Racak were KLA activists, and that's central to a count in this indictment, and that's why I say, going back to my earlier observation, that it shouldn't be adduced other than by the witnesses themselves. Now, I don't know if I've met Your Honour's various concerns. If I may say so, I've -- I understand them better than perhaps I did yesterday when I was last addressing them, particularly the point about the Prosecution taking a position, and I would invite you to allow that argument to be put back for general consideration, and my suspicion is that the -- or my guess is that the parties in both trials will -- and in respect of both witnesses invite a fuller consideration of the overall state of the evidence possibly in both trials before accepting that we are driven to the position in this particular type of case where we have to take a single stand. But that's for a later argument. As to the last point Your Honours made about the evidence coming in for particular purposes about the accused's state of mind and not being admitted, if that's the implication, for the truth of the content about the victims at Racak, that itself would require specific pointing by the accused that's where he's going and would still itself require of me or of those assisting in the Prosecution detailed investigation. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But because you would have to investigate the alleged corruption of the system, it would not be a basis for excluding this evidence. That goes to the heart of this case. Much more to the heart of the case than the facts of Racak do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour is right that it might not go to -- might not be a basis for excluding the evidence, if it's only to be admitted on the narrow basis, not the accused's basis. But I would still need time before I could deal with it in cross-examination for all the reasons I've advanced, not the least that I'm simply not in a position to -- I'm not disposed to nor really I think allowed to take positions on evidence until I know it's justified to take such a position. A matter of detail just going back to Dragan's evidence. I'm helpfully reminded by one of my colleagues that Dragan's organisation was largely dealing with, I think, undisputed facts like date of birth and place of death, allegedly undisputed but that sort of fact. And although there are many things that could be said about and indeed probably adverse to Dragan, in this particular role he was, as I've suggested, running something like a charity after the events dealing with what happened to people. Membership of the KLA at the hands of the Serbian judiciary is production of material by a party that may well have an interest particular to the events in this case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber's decision is that Mr. Jasovic may be called. We will make a further decision as to when he can be called and whether his evidence will be restricted to particular areas, and that decision we will make very soon, perhaps by tomorrow. So Mr. Jasovic doesn't need to be here today, Mr. Milosevic, and you should call another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreters still cannot hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is your microphone on, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, it is on now. I said I call witness Kosta Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So help me God on this day. I solemnly declare that on behalf of my own honour that I will speak the truth and nothing but the truth before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, first of all, please tell us where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1937 in the village of Dobrusa, municipality of Istok in northern Metohija. That is on the road between Pec and Kosovska Mitrovica. It is 12 kilometres away from Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us briefly what schools you completed and where.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in Vitomirica [Realtime transcript read in error "Vitina"] Near Pec, and secondary agricultural and mechanical school in Vinkovci in Croatia. Then I completed a higher school for the organisation of work in Belgrade, so my profession is engineer of professional safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just to correct the -- correct the transcript. Vitomirica is the place near Pec. In the transcript it says Vitina which is a completely different place.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it's far away from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you work after your education?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The first employment I had was in a factory in Pec and then at a sugar factory that was still under construction then in Pec. After that I got a job in the agricultural cooperative in Kosovo Polje, and then in the agricultural industrial combine of Kosmet Export in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During the Second World War, during the fascist occupation, your family was in Kosovo and Metohija where you all lived then; right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Dobrusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us briefly what happened to your family and your village during the fascist occupation of Yugoslavia and that area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when the occupiers came to Kosovska Mitrovica, they divided it into three zones. The occupiers divided it into three zones. The German occupation zone was in Kosovska Mitrovica, and Pec was the Italian occupation zone. So we were under the occupation of the Italian army. Since the Serb people were outlawed in Kosovo and Metohija, there were individual killings first and ultimately entire villages were attacked. Many villages throughout Metohija were torched in this way. There are very few villages that weren't. Only a few where the population was mixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Milosevic, kindly bring the witness to relevant evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many houses did your village number and was it a Serbian village?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a Serbian village. It had 384 houses to be exact, Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was your house set on fire?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And when we fled across some meadows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I indicated the witness should be asked questions that are relevant, that will adduce relevant evidence. This is not relevant evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very short introduction for us to see how the situation developed in general terms. So I'll get through that very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have had this kind of evidence before, this introductory, this historical narration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you this, then, Mr. Bulatovic, not of a historical nature, my next question, but in view of the fact that you said your house was set on fire, did you and the rest of the Serbs who were expelled from Kosovo and Metohija, did you ever come back after the war to live in your village?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. But that was before we were banned from returning and when the ban came into the force by the provisional government before the war had been -- had ended Popso Sljadovetrovic [phoen] signed this ban.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me what was life like after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No more. No more questions on that. I am not allowing any more questions on that. I am not allowing any more questions on that issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was the relationship between the Serbs and Albanians for several decades after the war? What I'm asking about is all the time after the war during that period of time while you were living in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in our village, a local board or committee was set up after the war, and the president was Ramalija [phoen] and somebody from a neighbouring village. Of the 380 houses none of the Serbs could be president of this board or committee which tells you what this new political thought on the part of the Communist Party was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me about the general relationships between Serbs and Albanians.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking the relationship between Serbs and Albanians immediately after World War II were tolerant. There was tolerance. They weren't bad, but the more time passed after the war the more the relations deteriorated. For example, workers -- farmers' cooperatives were performed in Serbian villages. I don't know of a single Albanian Siptar village who had -- which had farmers' cooperatives of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that international relations -- inter-ethnic relations were good.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time we could say that they were good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, to the best of your knowledge and experience when did these relationships begin to deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: They began to deteriorate after 1948, and the inform -- informbiro, when the population from Albanian began coming in under the guise of fleeing from Enver Hoxha's regime. They came to settle in Metohija and later on Kosovo. So this led to the first disturbances amongst the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened next? What was the next stage that you considered to be characteristic for raising tensions in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The next stage came when there were individual acts of violence and killings of certain people, and this led to disquiet among the population, especially when they learnt that Serbian land was being bought up, especially in the Decani, Djakovica and Prizren area and that this land was then given to the emigres from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And was 1968 a characteristic year in any way?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: 1968 was a characteristic year because there was an outpouring of demonstrations on the part of Albanians, pro-fascist in character, calling for slogans, reading Kosovo Republic. That was the motto of the demonstrations, that slogan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was in 1968, was it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was in 1968, when Tito was in Bugojno. And from there he sent a delegation, a party delegation to Kosovo to attend the ceremony there, and they were transported to Pristina by helicopter to quell the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you continue to live in Kosovo Polje after those demonstrations or did you decide to leave it and move out and settle somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: At that time we did think about leaving Kosovo, but we considered on the basis of the party conclusions, the conclusions made by party forums both in Serbia and Kosovo and Yugoslavia, that this would not repeat itself. We were given promises that this would not happen again, that there would be no more violence, nor would Serb lands be taken over forcibly or Serb houses taken over and other people settling in when they began to destroy houses and roofs were destroyed and so on. Then cautions were issued. Warnings were issued as in Vucitrn that this should not be done any more but these acts continued with unabated tempo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, how long did you yourself live in Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Kosovo Polje until about 1993 when I moved to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself are from Kosovo Polje and you say you lived there until around 1993 and then moved to Pristina. So that's quite near, is it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's seven kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Seven kilometres. Right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're both being asked to observe a pause between question and answer, Mr. Bulatovic and Mr. Milosevic, in the interest of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if this witness has evidence about the matters in the indictment, and I see from the 65 ter statement that he's to testify as to police and other armed activities during the war in Kosovo in the period referred to in the indictment. Bring the witness to that area. We have heard a lot of the background. We have sufficient background information on the matters leading up to the conflict. And if he is to testify about the military and police and armed activities in Kosovo in the period mentioned in the indictment, then let him do that immediately and don't waste time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, what you've just said can only be a typing error, because Mr. Bulatovic is not testifying about police matters. Perhaps you said politics and there was a typo error or something like that. But as far as the political situation in Kosovo is concerned and everything that went on, that's it. And among other things, Mr. Robinson, I should like to remind you that this witness here, Kosta Bulatovic was mentioned several times here in this courtroom as one of the leaders of the Serbian resistance movement and as a Serb nationalist. And he has spoken about the political situation in Kosovo and Metohija, and we see -- we shall see whether these qualifications are justified or not. Some groups in Kosovo were mentioned here a number of times. Kosta Bulatovic and others were mentioned in that regard, especially during the cross-examination when Mitar Balevic testified, that witness. So we now have the man, Kosta Bulatovic, and he will be able to tell us about all those events. But he had nothing to do, absolutely nothing to do with the police and is not testifying about police matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I merely read what is in the -- in the 65 ter. Perhaps it's an error. But in the witness schedule for this week it says, "Personal knowledge of military police and other armed activities during the war in Kosovo in the period referred to in the indictment." So I'm not certain whether that is a faithful transcription of what is in the 65 ter, but it does mention the police. In any event, I want the evidence to concentrate on the activities that are referred to in the indictment. We have had enough background information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you were a witness of the demonstrations both in the 1980s and 1990s in Kosovo. Tell us briefly, please, what effect did those demonstrations have on the conduct of the Serb population in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll be brief. Both in 1968 and in 1981, the demonstrations were the same, identical. And identical demands were made. They did not differ in any way except perhaps in the distribution of the people taking part in them. They were destructive in character, and of course as a minority nation in the province of Kosovo and Metohija, the Serb people were very much afraid because the authorities of the Kosovo and Metohija government or Serbia and Yugoslavia did not take any radical steps to address the situation and to prevent it and to bring law and order into the area to prevent any repetition. The leadership was expected to do that. The people expected them to do that, but it did not. It failed to take steps, and then the people were in a quandary what to do. And then at a meeting held in an old school building that has since been destroyed in Kosovo Polje, it was destroyed so that it should not be a monument to the first word spoken against terror against the Serbian people in Kosovo and Metohija at a meeting of the working people of Yugoslavia, because we have the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and the Socialist Alliance of the Working People of Yugoslavia, and I got up at that meeting. I was the first to get up and to criticise violence in general, and in particular I addressed the provincial organs and authorities. Neither the committees nor the state administration took any steps at all to combat violence and the perpetrators of violence. So the people accepted this, and as an honest citizen and individual, the people saw me and believed in me, and it -- why did they believe in me? Because the authorities this failed to take radical measures to deal with the situation. Then they wouldn't have needed Kosta Bulatovic or any other individual. So in a way, I became that first individual. I was not a leader of any kind. I was an ordinary citizen just as you see me here before you today. Nothing more than that. The only thing was that I publicly came out and looked truth in the eyes and told the organs of administration and the League of Communists of Kosovo and Metohija what I thought and what was situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you yourself, were you a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia? You were not, were you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I was for eight years, from 1958 to 1967, when I left the League of Communists for precisely these reasons, the reasons I am setting out here today at The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was it, Mr. Bulatovic, that you said that gained support from the citizens who heard you or, rather, let me put it this way: Can you in the briefest possible traits focus on the main points and elements of your speech? What was it you said?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. I'm going to stop this. Mr. Milosevic, I'm not satisfied that this is helpful. Mr. Nice, the accused made reference to a particular witness who mentioned Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Balevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In what areas?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's -- he's right that at that time we were exploring this general history, the period between 1966 and 1984, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 and the matters were reasonably fully explored there. Somewhere I've got a transcript of the Balevic evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is of course referred to in particular paragraphs in the indictment, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only by way of background matters, don't forget. And it's the background that's been adduced by the accused that we have been responding to and indeed content to respond to in a part because we accept that it's relevant to understand the accused's subsequent behaviour. But Your Honours will know that we have suggested as a starting point for any relevance 1966 or 1974, moving rapidly through to the mid-1980s as the points upon which we should be focusing attention as the earliest potentially significant points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just being shown by Judge Kwon the transcript where you said, Mr. Nice: "I'm grateful to hear Kosta Bulatovic is going to come. It will probably allow me to tailor the questions I'm going to ask this witness." Balevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, at this stage of the presentation of your defence, I personally find much of this inappropriate coming at this time. It is true -- it is true that particular issues were raised in relation to some background matters, but the question is whether we haven't heard enough of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When was this speech made, Mr. Bulatovic? What year was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was in 1983, thereabouts. It was after the demonstrations. We had to wait for the decisions of the state, what they were going to do after the demonstrations of the Siptars in 1981. So it was a year after or barely a year after the death of Comrade Tito. Now since they took no steps at all, then certain groups went to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. complain to Belgrade. Some groups went to the republican organs, for example; some went to the federal organs. At that time I was not -- not a functionary, didn't take part in any of that up to this meeting, but after the meeting I did. We went to complain to the Serbian authorities, especially when the cemetery in Sipolja was desecrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask, Mr. Milosevic, is he going to testify at all about the Kosovo conflict in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not about the conflict itself, no. Immediately before the conflict he was hospitalised in Pristina where he underwent treatment, and in the course of the conflict he was transferred to another hospital for rehabilitation. However, he can say something about the general conditions in that period of time. However, I would like to draw your attention, Mr. Robinson, to the fact that in the course of the testimony of Mr. Mitar Balevic, and I'm not saying that Mr. Balevic specifically named him, but in the course of Mr. Balevic's testimony, Mr. Nice pointed out that there existed a group of Serb nationalists led by Kosta Bulatovic, currently sitting before you. He also mentioned Miroslav Solevic and some other special role that they played, and this has to do with count 76, about which I will ask the witness later, because he attended that meeting as well. This is count 76 or paragraph 76 in the Kosovo indictment. At any rate, Mr. Nice claimed that there was a group of Serb nationalists there led by this very Kosta Bulatovic sitting across from you. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that this will be too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you have been proclaimed or portrayed as a man in conflict with authorities, some kind after conflict with authorities. However, based on my conversation with you, I did not conclude that there was indeed some kind of a conflict. However, you just mentioned a case in the village of Sipolja.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the evidence we are tendering through you, we have only two exhibits. One is a letter of residents of the village of Sipolja, and the other exhibit that we will discuss later is your personal request to move out. Now let us turn to this case in Sipolja. Please take a look. I think you have tab 1 before you. This is a letter which did not suit the then authorities. They did not look favourably upon it. And I will ask you to explain the reasons for that. This letter was signed by 18 citizens on the 30th of March, 1982, and it was delivered to the municipal authorities, provincial authorities, and republican authorities. So your municipality, province, and the republic. What is it that the residents of the village of Sipolja described as a problem? What did they petition the municipal and provincial authorities for? It is stated here that they wished to inform both the municipal, provincial, and the republican organs and ask for "protection that is guaranteed to us by the Constitution. We believe that our parents, brothers, sisters, relatives and others who are resting in peace in their graves should not be attacked." Is this the essence of the letter?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It is. May I elaborate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, Mr. Robinson, gentlemen: "We, the Serbian residents of Sipolja village were shocked to hear the news that our cemetery had been desecrated on the 28th of March, 1982. A group went to the cemetery and established that indeed 13 tombstones had been knocked down and damaged. Several days prior to this, wreaths and everything else in the cemetery that could be set on fire was torched."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no need to read it because we have the letter in front of us. If you have a specific question in relation to it then you may ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A very specific question which has to do with the atmosphere in Kosovo and Metohija at the time, Mr. Robinson. The cemetery was burned town. They are complaining to the municipal, provincial, and republican authorities and precisely because they were complaining they were labelled as the enemies of the state and Serb nationalists. Is that the consequence that ensued after you complained to the authorities?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the truth. And following that the cemetery in Bresje and Donji Petric was destroyed and the village in Petkovci was erased, was ploughed over. This can be found in the book Sleepless Night on page 216, a book written by Bogosavljevic. That was on the day when you listened to what the citizens had to say in Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bulatovic, who dictated the creation of such an atmosphere in which after complaining quite rightly so about an injustice you were labelled as Serb nationalists, people who were enemies of the state? Where were you qualified as such, by whom, by what type of authorities?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I was qualified as such by the municipal and provincial authorities of the province of Kosovo. And the grounds or, rather, what we established was that the -- those who defended the terror in Kosovo were those who served in the organs. They wanted to shut down not only me but the entire nation. They didn't want anybody to complain because at the time there was a one-party system in Yugoslavia. We did not have a multi-party system in Serbia at the time. That was introduced only when Mr. Milosevic came to power. In those days we had the dictate of just one party, and they wanted to intimidate not only me but the entire Serb population in Kosovo and Metohija. They had the stance that those who didn't like it could simply move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So this is an original -- this is the original letter. Nothing else was sent by you to them?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So in addition to this letter, what else was done in addition to you being qualified as Serb nationalists for sending this letter? What else was done? Did somebody react to that? Did somebody try to provide any assistance?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. There were simply decorative conclusions reached at the municipal and provincial committee to the effect that they would settle accounts with these enemies, that they would chase them into a foxhole and that they would do this and that. However, they did nothing. All of that was a simple lie. When you listened on the radio and when you read in the press what the authorities of the province were doing, you would have an impression that something is being done. What we asked for was not to be granted any greater rights in Kosovo and Metohija, no. We simply wanted to be equal with the Siptar nation and everybody else. There were Roma living there, Macedonians, Turks, and so on. We did not ask for greater rights. We simply wanted to be equal with them. And if this qualifies me as a nationalist, then yes, I'm sitting here before you and you can condemn me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bulatovic. What was the reaction of the Serb leadership to that? Did you go to Serbia to complain to somebody there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A group went to see the president of the Presidency whom we addressed as Comrade Ljubicic. He was a general. A group of people went to visit him and to acquaint him with what was happening in Kosovo and Metohija. However, nothing was done. They promised they would look into it, do this, do that. However, nothing came out of it. The following year another group in which I was went to see Dusan Ckrebic who was the president of the Presidency of Serbia. We spent two hours with him and informed him about many instances of violence and various methods that were used and covered up by authorities. The authorities kept threatening but did nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you went to see Nikola Ljubicic who was the president of the Presidency and later on that office was occupied by Dusan Ckrebic, and you went to see him as well?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he listened to you attentively and promised he would help?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he said he would help, but he said that Serbia had no competencies in the provinces because the provinces were not any more under the jurisdiction and competencies of Serbia, and the only thing they could do is to kindly ask the authorities in the province to see whether they would be willing to do something about it. Yes, that's how it was. However, we left empty-handed, left Belgrade and went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since this had to do with the Serbs and Montenegrins, you also went to Podgorica to complain to the authorities of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gave the initiative for us to go to Montenegro because I was hoping that they would have understanding for us as there were some Montenegrins living in Kosovo and Metohija. We went there and we did not see the then president of the Central Committee Culafic but were seen by two other people including Djoko Kovacevic. This dialogue that we had was taped on a videotape. There were eight of us in that meeting. They listened to us attentively, didn't promise us anything specifically, just said they would inform the Central Committee about this. However, as we were returning -- or, rather, upon our return to Pristina, we learned two days later about what was reported that we had said there and then they threatened that they would --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whom did they send this text to?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood. They sent this text to the provincial committee of the League of Communists of Kosovo. At the time, the province was not called Metohija because that referred to the lands owned by church and monasteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that statement of yours when you met with the leadership of Montenegro, what did you say, because you told us that after that meeting you were threatened by authorities that you would be arrested.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What they minded was not what was said there but the fact that we went to see them. They wanted to intimidate us so that we wouldn't go any further with this initiative. This is what they minded. The material that they read about the individual instances and so on was completely truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say there anything else other than what you had complained about earlier?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. We kept repeating the same story like parrots. However, nobody wanted to listen to our sad complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After that, after your visits, these consecutive visits to presidents of the Presidency of Serbia, Ljubicic and Ckrebic, and later on your visit to the leadership of Montenegro, did any changes occur afterwards?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to tell you. They would start issuing various threats saying they would put an end to this, and for a month it would be quiet. One wouldn't hear anything about the terror. However, afterwards, things would go back to normal. Violence would erupt. Terror would continue. People would be overcome by fear. At the time it wasn't allowed to state publicly things that I was stating, and people would come to my house because they believed that I was some kind of a powerful person who could solve the problems. However, I was just an ordinary citizen like everybody else. I had no special powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In all of these visits that you made, you did not skip the provincial authorities?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. As for our relationship with the provincial authorities, we did not address them in writing, no. We sent our people to them to inform them that we would have a meeting held that day and so on. And they would send their people from the provincial administration, and their people attended all of our meetings and gatherings. Nothing was done without the presence of authorities. And if somebody can prove otherwise, then they can see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you say that they attended all of your meetings and gatherings. And are you here referring to representatives of Prosecution authorities?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Provincial and municipal authorities would come to our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these representatives, were they also -- were they both Serbs and Albanians?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was always a mixed composition. There would always be Serbs and Albanians in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What do you know about the petition that was sent by 2.000 Serbs in 1985? This was a petition published in the press.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1984 when we realised that nobody really helped us, nobody really paid attention to our complaints, we said, all right, let's write a petition. And the text of this first petition was not published anywhere because only 78 Serbian citizens signed it. People didn't dare sign such documents, gentlemen. Therefore, we decided not to submit this petition. A year late where we realised things were not going well for us, we met once again to discuss things with Dobrica Cosic, the writer, because we were so desperate. We went to the state. We went to the party. Nobody would pay attention to us, so we went to see this writer and he told us, "Whatever you did, you did this wisely. You addressed yourself to your state, to your leadership, to your authorities, and that is the proper procedure. This does not involve any kind of illegal activities." And he said, "Why don't you write a petition?" And I said, "Yes, well, we did write a petition but only 78 people signed it." And he said, "Why don't you write a new petition and include all your requests about what changes ought to be implemented. And I think that the terror that the Serb population in Kosovo was exposed to has increased and people have realised it. So why don't you go ahead with this." So we indeed did, and 2.600 Serbs signed this petition. When the journalists asked the MPs in the Assembly of Yugoslavia about the number of signatures, they said 2.016, and there were also some other figures given, whereas the actual figure was 6.200. And, Mr. Robinson, let me tell you, that later over 86.000 residents of Serb ethnicity in Kosovo and Metohija signed this petition as well. In a village near Orahovac I submitted the text of the letter and the petition written by Kole Shiroka. I submitted this written by Colonel Filipovic, and we submitted this to Kole Shiroka who was an Albanian highly positioned in the government. Later on, they found the text of this petition as a result of which on the 2nd of April, 1986, I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bulatovic. Let us pause here. So this petition was published in the press.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how come you were arrested because a text of the petition published in the press was found on you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: They believed that if they arrest me, they will shut up everyone else in Kosovo and Metohija. Nobody else would dare speak the truth. All those who didn't like the situation could simply leave. That was their position. And this is why all of this all came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you were arrested in order to intimidate other -- others who signed the petition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just let the witness answer this question and then we'll take the break for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have here the text of the petition, and with your permission, Your Honours, I can read it to you so that you can see for yourself that it contains nothing that is aimed at any other nation or ethnic minority. All we wanted is to be granted equal status, equal to what our neighbours and other residents had. And this was the multi-ethnicity that we sought, the multi-ethnicity that the entire world insists upon. This was not a case of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it in Serbian, the petition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I'm in a position to provide an English translation for you later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. When we return we'll have a look at that. We will adjourn for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the document that I have in translation is the same as the document from which the witness was just about to read, I'm happy for it to be available. It comes printed in a textbook as so often these documents are rather than the original version, and the Court might think it prudent to ask the witness it read perhaps from the first paragraph to check that we're on the same general --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With due apologies to you and the witness, for purely technical reasons can I receive information about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Jasovic? Can he testify on Tuesday or are you going to decide on some other date? It would suit me if he could testify on Tuesday, and Mr. Nice will have enough time to read all of his documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, have you confirmed with the Victims and Witnesses Unit whether Mr. Jasovic would be in The Hague to testify on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can be in The Hague, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in response to the accused's observation that I will have time to read the statements, two points. First of all, the scale of my preparation and investigation depends on the ruling that the Court is going to make, but even so, apparently reading go the statements fully - I've only skimmed through some of them - is, you know, a very considerable time-consuming exercise, and as it happens every minute of my time between the close of business today and start of business on Tuesday is already fully committed, including the weekend, to work at the Tribunal, so that I can't devote any time to it. But the principal problem is that we simply don't know what level of investigation will be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We might decide to hear him in chief on Tuesday, postponing the cross-examination, and tomorrow we will give a decision as to whether the evidence in chief would be confined in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's always a possibility. I've indicated earlier that it's one that I've tried always personally to avoid because of the build-up of outstanding cross-examination and having to revisit earlier testimonies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think this is the only case we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. It happened the other way around in the Prosecution case quite a lot and having to go back to issues and remind ourselves is not very satisfactory. Also -- well, it does mean that there will be no time for me to consider your ruling and the terms of the admissibility between the ruling and the calling of the witness. But I -- otherwise I can't object to evidence being given in chief if I have postponed cross-examination, but I encourage the Chamber to make a different decision if it can. Of course it may be that the accused's problem is he simply doesn't have any other witnesses. If that is his position and if he says so candidly that might help the Chamber. I have to say that we haven't received an up-to-date list of witnesses, and there is some uncertainty in our mind as to who comes next, another problem that we're going to have to face with our resources between now and Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you have any other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One who was on the list got sick so he won't be able to testify immediately. He will testify somewhat later. But the rest are fine, and we can take them in the right order. And Jasovic is on the list too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will it be inconvenient for Mr. Jasovic if we were to take his testimony in chief on Tuesday, postponing the cross-examination, so that he would have to return?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that would not really cause any special problem. He could come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, what we'll do is hear Mr. Jasovic on Tuesday in chief. Cross-examination will be postponed to a date to be fixed, and tomorrow we will indicate by order whether the examination-in-chief is to be confined to any particular area. Now we go back to Mr. Bulatovic and the petition.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this paper that Mr. Nice distributed. That's not the same petition. This is the petition of the intellectuals of Belgrade. And already on page 1 reference is made to the following: In October 1985, 2.016 Serbs from Kosovo and Metohija sent petitions to the Assemblies of Serbia and Yugoslavia respectively. So there is only mention of the petition that Mr. Bulatovic is speaking about, but Mr. Bulatovic's petition is from January 1986. Also, it is addressed to the Assembly of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia in 1986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. You say it's not the same petition, so we can't rely on this. We'll then have to have the petition read, those pertinent parts, so that they can be translated. What is it that you wanted out of the petition?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted only -- I mean, I did not even include the petition in my exhibits because it was generally known. What I wanted to get out of it was anything that could be qualified as Serb nationalism, something that the leadership in Kosovo and Metohija could respond to in such a forceful way as they did and qualify it the way they did. So my question would be whether there is any such thing contained in the petition. Mr. Bulatovic has the petition here in this book that was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bulatovic, is there anything in the petition that could be qualified as Serb nationalism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There isn't, Mr. Robinson. The text of this petition sought to rectify everything that was wrong in society so that we would be brought onto an equal footing with others, other peoples in Kosovo and Metohija, the Siptars in particular in Kosovo and Metohija. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't need to have it read. If Mr. Nice wishes to cross-examine on it, then he can of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I possibly trouble the witness just for the cite of the extract from the book at the moment because if it's not the version that I've laid before you I'll possibly be able to find it between now and next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please return it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, did you sign this petition?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I am the first signatory of this petition, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, since you are the first signatory --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- was this an expression of your autonomous position of you who wrote and signed this petition, or did you receive some instructions from some authority or some organisation or some individuals in terms of how you should draft it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to say before this Tribunal, as I swore that I would speak the truth, we drafted the text of the petition. We ordinary people, ordinary citizens from different walks of life. We were not lawyers. We called a journalist to help us, Rajko Djurdjevic from Kalidzerica [phoen] near Belgrade, and he finalised the text for us, and I typed it out and I put my address on it and I was the first person to sign it. And you can see that in the book that Mr. Nice has right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Bulatovic, how was this petition received in the Yugoslav public?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In a negative way among certain forms, especially in Kosovo and Metohija and also at the level of the federation. It was qualified as some kind of revival of some kind of Serbian nationalism in Kosovo. How was it that we were seeking to have an equal position in Kosovo now? Are you not equal? That's what they were saying. They thought that what was being done in Kosovo and Metohija, that is to say, this terror and the tacit support of terror by the authorities was something that should not be changed in the society. I don't know if I was clear when I said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you were quite clear and that will suffice. Tell me, you said that together you wrote the drafts of this petition and you wrote it. Who else was involved in this with you in preparing this petition?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This petition, in addition to myself, was prepared by Bosko Budimirovic, Solevic. The text of the petition, in addition to myself it was prepared by Milo Maslar Popovic [phoen] who is here on this picture. Would it be possible to put on the overhead projector the picture of all these men so that the Court can see them? So they can see that these are ordinary citizens. All these complaints that were coming from the grassroots, that is something that we wanted to put down in this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think we wish to see the photograph, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see. All right. All right. It's for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Solevic Budimirovic. Your name was mentioned, Solevic's, Budimirovic's.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And some others who were the core of all of this. Perhaps it would be better if you were to explain how they described you. Was all of this related to preparation of this petition?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Termed us Serb nationalists but not in terms of nationalism but in terms of chauvinism, hatred, and there was none of that, because a nationalist is a person who defends his people and who loves his people, and a chauvinist is a person who hates all other people and love only their own people, and they were trying to say we were the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As for these people you mentioned along with yourself, did you set up an informal group in order to meet and to organise your work, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, there was no group. All of this was spontaneous because I was the first one to speak up about this violence in public. People kept coming to my home all the time. There were streams of people coming in from all over Kosovo and Metohija. Kosovo and Metohija is so big. It has -- it covers an area of 10.804 square kilometres. So can you imagine people coming from all over to see me? And who was I? I was never in any kind of government. I wasn't even on the workers' council in my factory. I was just an engineer who did his own job in the overhaul department. I was head of the department for a while, and also I was chief of the rolling stock of the company for a while too. And there were Siptars and Turks and Romany who were employed there at the time. And I would like to say publicly before this Tribunal that if we look at my entire career and my entire life, I was born there, and I lived there for 62 years. If there is anyone who has a single word to say, let them speak up and let them send a telegram or whatever to this Tribunal and say what it is they have to say against me. Now, if I bother people because I can speak up and say publicly something is wrong, that is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you lived in Kosovo for a long time and you mentioned that you worked with people belonging to different ethnic groups. Let me single out of the Albanians now. Do you believe that there is a single Albanian who you put in harm's way in any way?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Heaven forbid. I was brought up by the Bulatovic family and that is the biggest Serb clan, and we are the descendants of Vojvodan Niksa, and the town of Niksic in Montenegro today was named after him. And we are supposed to speak in a humane manner and we are supposed to treat people in a humane manner. Because if I do harm to somebody else, I'm also in another way harm my own family and my own country. That is how we were all brought up, and that is why we always got into trouble because we could not fit into all these things that were happening here and there. We move along a straight line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, in relation to all of this, when these petitions were made and we see later there was this petition of the Serb intellectuals --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- and you said that you addressed the state authorities in Serbian and Montenegro in the municipality in Kosovo, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any improvement in terms of redressing all these situations on account of which you protested?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President and gentlemen of the court, nothing was improved. And that was the problem. When you saw the public media and you saw what the leaderships of the province were saying, you would think that it would be all honey and milk in Kosovo and Metohija, but nothing was really done. They had some personnel changes within different structures of government. The policy remained the same. And it was the political postulates that were the problem. It wasn't the problem of whether it was Kosta Bulatovic personally who was there or some other person who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bulatovic. Just before we took the break you mentioned that you had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did that happen and why?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I was arrested on account of this petition that is now in this book that Mr. Nice has right now, and the reason was that they wanted to stop me in a way. They thought that if they would stop me if they did not let me speak in public any longer nobody else would protest in Kosovo and Metohija. People were moving out. Whoever could sell his land, his property, his house, whatever, people were selling it for peanuts, and they were moving onto central Serbia because they were trying to get away from this territory. They thought that that trend should continue. I spoke in public, and I was the initiator of this document, this petition, so I was a hindrance to them from this political point of view, not from any other point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bulatovic. This arrest of yours, did it receive any kind of publicity?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did receive publicity. There were reactions. I was in detention in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why did they arrest you? How did they explain this?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was spreading a rebellion among the people, inciting the people to rise, but they did not mention the petition because they wanted to conceal what they themselves were doing. And then tens of thousands of people assembled around my house and I never knew all these people. And then it turned out that I was in Prizren. I did not know what was going on outside, and then there were tens of thousands of people who were gathering there. The masses did not disperse within three days and nights. And then they were they were afraid that there would be an all-out rebellion among the people and that there would be some undesirable consequences of all this of altogether different proportions and that is why they released me ultimately. Then the then President of Serbia, Ivan Stambolic, the late Ivan Stambolic now, he came to Kosovo Polje on the 6th of April. He made a speech there in front of the cultural centre, and this is characteristic of politicians from these times of communism. The people were not happy with that. And then during his speech people would start chanting, "Kosta, Kosta." That bothered him quite a great deal, and he was wondering who this Kosta was and who was it who was disrupting their political game. He promised that measures would be taken like all other leaders from the province promised. And he gave promises on behalf of Serbia, that further violence would be prevented, that all of this would be stopped, that there would be an alleviation of the situation, that we'd continue to live together as brothers, et cetera. However, when he left nothing changed. And after a year, after a bit more than a year, after he left or, rather, the following day after he left, several thousand people went to the Sava centre in Belgrade. I have a photograph from that gathering here too. And an old man, aged 83, speaks here. Since I cannot place it on the overhead projector, let the Court see this. This is Bozo Markovic from the village of Batusa. That is where they cut off electricity right now. Well, this old man died in the meantime, but he's the one who spoke at the Sava centre now, and I happen to have his photograph here with me. After that, a little over a year later in fact, Zoran Grujic - he's a doctor of science -

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, please. Before you go on to tell us about Zoran Grujic, tell us this, please. Mr. Bulatovic, how long were you in prison on that occasion when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, three days. And then there was this rally by the people and you released; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever arrested on another occasion?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That same year on the 20th of June 1986 I was arrested in the village of Baric, not far from Obrenovac. Because on that day the people from several villages in Kosovo and Metohija, there was an exodus of these people towards Serbia and Krusevac, and the police stopped this exodus. They stopped them and there are photographs to bear that out. We can take a look at them here or attach them to the rest of the evidence here showing that the police stopped them at Kosovo Polje and did not allow the people to carry on in that direction. And for that reason, I was arrested there because anything that happened after I first spoke out in 1983 or 1984, whenever that was, I think it was 1983, everything that happened in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Kosovo and Metohija after that I was the scapegoat every time. Everything else was considered to be fine in the state, but this was the one element that led to discord. So I was arrested, and all this was at the end of November or the beginning of November 1987. You arrived I think after Zoran Grujic was expelled from Kosovo, I believe, and they burnt down five of his houses in Kosovo Polje that he and his brother had there. And you can see the remnants of the walls of those houses. But he he's now the director of the commercial bank in Gracanica, that same Dr. Grujic now. Anyway, the people rallied in front of his house, and because they were protesting why he had to flee to Belgrade and the people said why don't you go over there --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Bulatovic. You say that the people rallied around Zoran Grujic's house to protest for the fact that he had had to flee to Belgrade. That was the reason they were -- had gathered there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That's why they gathered there. Now let me tell you what happened there. When I arrived I came across Mitar Balevic and a member of the communal committee of Pristina, Pavle Jovanovic; he's died in the meantime. But he was an activist, he was a decent and honest man from our village and our general area. Anyway, they were there to talk to the people to decide what they were going to do and then somebody put forward a proposal, that is to say, Svetozar Grujic village, that they said we called Ivan Stambolic to come last year but he did nothing. Now we're going to call you. You were the president at the time of the Central Committee of Serbia. I believe so. We -- somebody proposed that we call you and that was the decision made, let's call this man Milosevic. He was not generally known to the public at large at that time. But anyway, you had come from the Municipal Committee and had nothing to do with Kosovo but we decided to call you. That's where the decision was made, and Mitar Balevic always the president of the local committee from Kosovo Polje took it upon himself and pledged before those people there, he guaranteed that he would inform the Central Committee of Serbia about all the goings-on and the decisions made and that we would request that Slobodan Milosevic come to Kosovo Polje at the invitation of the populace. And on the 20th, I believe it was the 20th of April you yourself. Arrived somewhere in the afternoon you arrived in Kosovo Polje. You went on foot from the centre of Kosovo Polje, the central cultural centre there and to the Aca Marovic music school building. You got up onto the stage there and addressed the people. There weren't too many people, just about 10.000 people. And when you delivered your address the people were not satisfied, Mr. President, with your speech, with what you were saying there Mr. President. And then Solevic as the president of the conference of the 17th local commune shouted out from amongst the crowd - he was close to the stage but he's taller than me - he said, Comrade president we didn't call you here to listen to a monologue. We invited you here to hold a dialogue with you. That means that we want -- want to tell you our problems and then you can relate to that. And you responded. The meeting was over. You said Wait for me in four days time, elect your representatives and I'll be back. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, put specific questions. And I would be grateful for shorter answers, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, so I addressed the citizens. You have explained to us now that Solevic said he didn't wish to listen to a monologue but he wanted to enter into a dialogue. And I said very well, then. You elect your representatives because you can't have a dialogue at a rally but I'll be back and then we'll be able to hold a dialogue. That's the truth of it. And did I come back in four days' time?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I'm now going to read what it says in para 76 of the Kosovo indictment with respect to that particular rally that took place in April 1987. I'm going to skip over where it says that I've been elected as chairman, et cetera, et cetera, in 1986. And then they go on to say "In meetings with local Serb leaders and in a speech before a crowd of Serbs, Slobodan Milosevic endorsed a Serbian nationalist agenda." Now, I'm going to ask you something quite specific. Did you have any agenda at all, any kind of agenda at that meeting? You were at the cultural centre meeting in Kosovo Polje where I spoke. You were there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you: Did you have any kind of agenda, any kind of agenda at all?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We had no kind much agenda except what we set out in the petition asking us to be treated on a foot of equality with the other nations and nationalities living in Kosovo and Metohija. Our overall demands were reduced to that one demand and there was no agenda. No programme of any kind. You listened. 70 people presented their problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me, what was the purpose of that rally of that meeting? Was it for you to hear me or for me to hear you? And what in fact was the object of the meeting? You had elected your representatives and the cultural centre was pack jammed, it was full.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was like this. We had our expectations. We expected the people who had been harmed in any way or disadvantaged in any way or where violence had been committed against individuals in Kosovo and Metohija that they should tell you of their troubles. But we also expected of you, believe me, we wanted to hear you tell us whether there was any hope, whether the leadership of Serbia would do anything to help us, otherwise that there would be a collective exodus. And let me say before I go on - and this is something that doesn't exist in my statement - we saw that we were left to -- blind forces that nobody was going to help us. Mr. Robinson, we went in groups. I, for example, went to Paracin with Anko Djuro Bauk and Bosko Mirovic and we went to see the mayor there to see whether he could do anything to help us, give us some social land, social land where we would be able to build our houses and move out of the area we lived in and to move there to avoid this general exodus. So that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to that rally in Kosovo Polje. You were at the cultural centre in Kosovo Polje on the 24th of April, were you not?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as the meeting started, the rally started, you could hear a lot of noise and some sort of moans. And Mitar Balevic said Comrade President, that's how we addressed you at the time, outside the situation is very tense. People are debating. You must go outside and calm them down. And you and Asim Vllasi went outside together. I did not go outside. I remained in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So aim note going to ask you about any of that further what happened outside because you say you weren't there yourself. And we were able to see what happened on the tapes here?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes I listened to the tapes too, yes. Yes, yes. Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Anyway, the situation did calm down. The meeting went on throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, until 6.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people took the floor at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Over 70, certainly. Now the exact number I really do not wish to hazard a guess. But certainly over 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us how the meeting evolved? Was it peaceful?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, peaceful, with dignity. There were no excessive situations. Everything was set out nicely. You were there; Azem Vllasi, president of the provincial committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia was there; Kole Shiroka, the late Kohl Shiroka was there. He was the representative from the federation. He was there. Then there was Haliti what's-his-name, the president of the Municipal Committee of the League of Communists of Pristina.
