And with them they had several other people escorting them. But you were in the first row I was in the seventh row and I was able to see all that very well. I wasn't a speaker at the meeting, of course, because I personally was not harmed or didn't have any adverse things happen to me, so I didn't want to speak up although perhaps if I was in another country I might have spoken up, but I didn't want to focus on my observe problems. I wanted to let the people set out the general problems, the problems they were having.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Bulatovic. Now before I ask you any more questions, I'd like to draw your attention to a document here. It is to be found in tab 2. It is your request; right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that you addressed it to the council of the 16th and 17th local communes of Kosovo Polje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it also says that this demand or request --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You sent this on the 12th of November, 1987, did you not?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was seven months after you had been in Kosovo Polje yourself, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me this, please. Can we see on the last page here that you addressed this to the alliance of the 16th and 17th Local Communes of Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That you also sent copies to the regional conference of Kosovo Polje? We can see that as well. The action conference of the local commune?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The organisation of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia of the 16th and 17th Local Communes, the District Conference of the People's Alliance of Kosovo Polje, the conferences of the local communes in Kosovo Polje, all sub-branches in Kosovo Polje. All in all taken together, all these are the addresses that this was sent to. They're all in Kosovo Polje, and at the end it says "To the people to whom I belong and the public for information."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because you wanted this to be published?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If the need arose, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just briefly now deal with what you set out here and what your demands were. You say, for example, the following: You wanted to be allowed to leave your place of residence, and you stipulate in the last paragraph on page 1 that you were unlawfully arrested on the 2nd of April, 1986 and released on the 5th of April, 1986 with the explanation a mistake had been made in your case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that all further prosecution would be discontinued?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, there were complications later on - I don't want to enter into those now - you described them anyway. And then in September you wrote to the leaders and all the Albanians, Kole Shiroka, Azem Vllasi, Rahman Morina and Dr. Ragip Halili, you addressed them, requesting that your case be closed. Shiroka was in the federation; Vllasi in the province; Morina and Halili, president of the Municipal Committee of Pristina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After that, you say that on the -- you addressed them on the 8th of September, and on the 10th of September, that is the last paragraph on page 2, I'm going to read it out: "On the 10th of September, the inspector from Pristina came to see me in the company, the state security inspector, with a request that I come with him or that I go myself to the provincial Secretariat of the Interior because some comrades from the republic and the federation needed to talk to me about something."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I went there with him to the office of Comrade Bozovic where the comrades from the Republic of Serbian Federation were, and I talked to them. Who were those comrades?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the man from the federation was Raukovic, that that was his surname, Raukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What organs were they from?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: They were from the state security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So they were security people?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes. And Savic was from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say: "They said that I was the organiser of the gathering of the Serbian people in Kosovo and demanded in future that I should not go to such gatherings or speak at them because my presence and my speech aggravated the crowds and many who did not even know me. I answered that I was not any sort of organiser of the gatherings because it was the worries and troubles that were rallying those people. And as far as my speeches were concerned, I stood by them because I only spoke the simplest truth about what was being done against that people in Kosovo and that I did not persuade or instruct anybody to any gathering or speech-making."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I promised them then I would not go to gatherings or speak about anything whatsoever and that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, time for a question. You're not in a reading class.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, you then promised that you wouldn't go to any gatherings, that you wouldn't even speak, and did you do so? Did you go to gatherings? Did you speak?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I went to gatherings and I did speak. I went to Niksic to attend a gathering of that kind and I spoke there. And at home, when I came back from the interview in Pristina, there were a 150 to 200 citizens gathered there. When I had been taken to Pristina by the state security. Now, the next day I called Bozovic up and told him to send his men and asked them why the people had gathered there and what they wanted. The next day there were about 2.000 citizens who had gathered there, and then I had to come out before them and to address then publicly and to explain them -- to explain to them what had happened and to ask them to go home. I said that things would get better, would improve. So I persuaded my people by using this ruse to calm the situation down. That's what I had to tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had to convince them to go home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to go home. That's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then here in your demands where you ask to be allowed to move out, you go on to say that after the 2nd, 3rd and 4th of April while you were in detention the citizens rallied in front of your house. And you said: "I ask you, how could I have organised any kind of gathering in Kosovo Polje from prison?" So you're justifying yourself because of this rally. Now, was this rally something that was unlawful which would need justification?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not illegal or unlawful, Mr. President and Mr. Robinson. They were methods. They didn't know what to do, so this was the method they chose, whether to liquidate me physically or let me to leave the territory. However, at that time they placed a ban on anybody leaving Kosovo without requests put in to the local commune. That is why I addressed this to both the local communes of Kosovo Polje, this request of mine. So the people had gathered there because of the troubles they had encountered. We all had the same troubles and problems. We didn't know what would become of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this document where you asked to be allowed to move out, on page 4, paragraph 1, you say that pressure was exerted on your family: "My family has also come under pressure..." you say. And then you go on to speak about your daughters and how they were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that something that happened only to you at the time or did it happen to other people as well, to anybody else in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It happened -- it was the order of the day. It -- they wanted to silence me in a way, and these were -- this was one of the methods they applied. I have no words to express what went on during that period of time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you then complain why a certain official who was either a Serb or Montenegrin; I can see by the surname.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Stijovic. He's not an Albanian. He labelled you as speaking from nationalistic positions and then in response you say at the end of that second paragraph: "In defending my people and demanding their rights, only on the basis of full equality in Socialist Yugoslavia, I am also defending other peoples, demanding their rights, only on the basis of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. full equality, without which there can be no 'brotherhood and unity'."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I always said and publicly at every single meeting. And precisely because of the fact that they couldn't find anything wrong with something like that to lock me up and to have me do hard labour, I was a very difficult adversary for them in the ring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Bulatovic. So you advocated nothing but equality. You did not want greater rights. Was that the position of other people who together with you wrote petitions? Was there any incitement of animosity towards Albanians or any other national community in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Robinson, I maintain here with full certainty that I tried to educate everybody who came it my house, who came to my offers, who stopped me in the street and in all kinds of other places. I always told them that if we do anything bad or say anything bad against the Siptars, Romas, Turks or anybody else living in Kosovo and Metohija. That by doing so we would indirectly become enemies of our own people and nobody who held such beliefs should come and see me. So they knew it. I told them, I would disown you. I would not speak to you again if any of you dares to say anything extreme. It is true that we are threatened, it is true that we are subjected to terror. However, we have no other country but Serbia and we cannot flee our own country. We have to be tolerant. We have to live here in such a way as to spread tolerance and in such a way as to force the state leadership to do something about this, not individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bulatovic. We will skip over several years, after which there were constitutional amendments in 1989. I assume that you remember that.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are no constitutional expert, therefore, I will ask you nothing about constitutional amendments. I simply wish to ask you: How did you as a citizen in Kosovo and Metohija see these amendments and changes based on what you experienced, based on your talks with your neighbours and friends, and tell us how did Albanians view these amendments?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In a normal way. The initial period, when these amendments were introduced, was a calm one. There were no incidents. There was no violence immediately. However, after some time lapsed, all of a sudden Albanians started leaving their offices, their companies, Mr. Robinson. We ordinary citizens were surprised. We were wondering how is it. It was so hard to get a job and once you did get a job, why would you leave your job? How would you support your family if you had no job? We could not understand that they were being funded, from other countries, from other states, through other channels that are known only to them and I know nothing about. So we were wondering where were all these huge funds coming that enabled them not to work but live well. The living standard of Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija and that of Siptars in Kosovo and Metohija was very different, and it was more beneficial for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you have said that you wondered how the Albanians could be leaving their jobs because it was so hard to get a job.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you could not understand that they were being funded, "from other countries, from other states, through other channels only known to them, and I know nothing about them." So what is the source of your information that they were being funded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They -- the newspapers wrote about that, namely that they were being funded from the Middle East flew drug trafficking channels and arms trade. This is what our papers are writing about and probably press in other states as well. This is the only source of information for me. I don't have an intelligence agency to inform me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bulatovic, so you told us about this phenomenon, namely that many Albanians were leaving their jobs for reasons known only to them. Do you know that in their political circles at the time it was advocated that they ought to boycott their jobs and other aspects? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. On one occasion Kacusha Jashari and Azem Vllasi practically publicly called them to boycott which surprised the entire Yugoslav public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bulatovic, please tell us, was there anyone in the state leadership or anyone among Serbs in Kosovo urging Albanians to leave their jobs? Was there anyone firing them, dismissing them from their jobs? You lived there at the time. Do you know of any cases where they were dismissed from their jobs by Serbs, not Albanians?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: God forbid. If such an information existed, then it needs to be specified as to where, when and how. This is a tremendous lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the establishment of parallel structures in health services, in education by Albanian organisations?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I know that they pulled out students from schools and took them to private homes where they organised schooling for them. I saw that in Obilic. There was a house there where they had their school where their students went. They taught them there. The circle of those who supported boycott of all views of public life was spreading. We at the time did not know that they had -- that they were receiving assistance from outside. There were Albanians who were good neighbours of ours, good colleagues. We worked together. We had no kind of problem between us. However, such Albanians did not receive support. Rather, those who wanted to spread error and violence received support. That was the faction that received support, whereas the other faction was neglected, and this is why in this latest war they came to kill all of those individuals who supported friendly relations with Serbs and good neighbourly relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you get this information that they were killing certain of their own?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have a story that was published in this paper where a man in Brolic was moved from that place -- that's not -- in the municipality of Decani, and later on moved out to Montenegro. This man and his daughter were killed subsequently. And this is the man who had excellent relations with the Serbs. They had nothing but respect for each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you believe he was killed because he had a positive attitude towards Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is published in the newspaper called Tanjug.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No need to quote. We know that those people who had any sort of positive attitude towards Serbs were punished.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely true. And they know it better than anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bulatovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... leading questions recently. Perhaps he could be subsequently reminded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes, the tenancy to lead is still there. You have to avoid leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, in the course of these ten years starting in 1989 until 1999, there were constitutional amendments in 1989?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you spent the entire time in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, until the 26th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And you worked throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was retired, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since when?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You had numerous contacts with Serbs and Albanians?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally. They were my neighbours. They lived in my neighbourhood. And when I was brought from hospital to the apartment in Pristina, even Albanian neighbours came to visit me when I was sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So during those ten years, do you know of any cases where Serbs dismissed Albanians from work or in any way discriminated against them?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I saw from 200 to 500 people every day. I never heard such information. And if anybody possesses such information, they should acquaint me with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Where were you when the aggression on Yugoslavia started?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of March, 1999, I was involved in a very serious accident, traffic accident, and I was in the orthopaedic clinic of the hospital centre in Pristina. I was -- I had been operated on and was in intensive care, and the bombing started on the 24th of March when I was in still in intensive care.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And in late May you were transferred to Igalo?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that entire time you spent in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was in the hospital for about ten days and then I went to Nis for rehabilitation there and then I returned back to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. During those ten days that you were in hospital, did you observe what the ethnic composition of the doctors and patients were in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just like before the aggression, that was the composition while I was there. The same people were there. Here, you can see this arm of mine. It was treated by an Albanian doctor, healed by an Albanian doctor. There were many Albanians there. There was a Turkish nurse there who administered treatment. And they behaved normally even though rounds were falling left and right. There was nothing wrong there while I was there. I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened after your stay at the hospital? You went someplace else?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the rehabilitation centre in Nis where I was treated by Dr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have to go into details.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And then afterwards I was sent home, spent there ten days, and Dr. Popara ensured that there be an ambulance car to take me to Igalo, to Montenegro, to the coast, because I wasn't able to go there any other way. And this is where I was when the Kumanovo agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You as a person of -- who lived in Kosovo and Metohija, who was a citizen of Kosovo and Metohija and who experienced himself all kinds of inter-ethnic relations that existed in Kosovo and Metohija, please tell us how did you see the police activity in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it as something quite normal and natural. A number of Serbs had been killed starting with Djordje Bjelic who was killed on the steps and then there were two people killed in Mejolic [phoen], and the killing of Serbs started to be very widespread which means that the police had to go out and intervene. They had to block traffic to prevent the terrorists from moving about. They killed policemen in Glogovac. Seven or nine policemen were killed at the roadblock. A relative of mine, Bulatovic, was taken out of the train and killed, and his wife watched from the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You had contact with many Albanians. What was the position of the Albanians that you communicated with during the NATO aggression? What was their position with respect to NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. Their reaction was not a bad one, Mr. President, and I would be unfair if I said otherwise. They said the same thing that we did, that this was no good no good either for Serbs or for Albanians and that it would lead to nothing. However, these were Albanians who were not members of this fascist-like organisation, and I could not be friends with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You remember that Serbs were going in large numbers to take part in demonstrations in 1988 and 1989. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What do you know about these cases of Serbs going there? Were there any leaders who urged them to take part in that or who asked you from Kosovo and Metohija to travel to other cities to demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. We did this on our own. We first went to Novi Sad because Krunic and the Vojvodina leadership were quite a hindrance to constitutional amendments in Serbia which were supposed to put the provinces under the jurisdiction of Serbia. So we attended those rallies. We went to various cities. And simply speaking, Mr. President, we went to organise rallies in those cities so that our people could let everyone know about what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija. The press at the time wrote very little about Kosovo and Metohija, and if they wrote something at all it was not written on the front page. So we didn't know anybody, Mr. President. Did you know any of those people from Kosovo Polje? Did you know anybody from Kosovo? We don't know anyone either. The only person that we knew in Belgrade was the person that I went to see in Belgrade because I was the first one to go. I first went to Zarija Matilovic [phoen]. I went to Batric Jovanovic. These were people who were MPs, who were deputies in the Assembly. In the west you call them congressmen. So I went to see them in order to inform them about the situation, to show evidence about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In those rallies organised by Serbs in 1988 and 1989, was the main reason for organising these rallies to inform the public with what was going on or did you have perhaps some other goals?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. That was our only goal because we wanted the people to realise what was going on. For 50 years they've been telling us that there was brotherhood and unity there, that everything was cream and peaches. However that was not true. Only we knew what we suffered. Nobody could believe that. Nobody could even fathom something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bulatovic. Was there any violence in any of those rallies?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you. Was there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard of any violence. And if somebody claims otherwise, tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Bulatovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you have testified that you got along very well with Albanians when you were in the hospital, you were visited by Albanians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Outside of the hospital as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have had evidence of this kind before. So what really caused the conflict in Kosovo? If there was this brotherhood and everybody was getting along well, what really was the trigger for this conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The trigger of the conflict was their programme, their fascist-like programme, because a large number of Balists, fascists who had sided up with the fascists, with the Italians. They simply moved on to the partisan units. They were taken over by the partisan units. They accepted to become members of the then Communist Party of Yugoslavia. At that time they behaved very honestly, very decently. They were quite simply very loyal at the time, at the beginning. At that time, Mr. Robinson, there weren't any major problems. Perhaps somewhere, but that happens in any country and that could be tolerated. However, as we moved on from the Second World War, then these worms started squirming and they were receiving some kind of support. We first felt this wave after the Cominform Resolution in 1948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They whom? The Albanian people or a party --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Terrorists. They're terrorists. Yes, yes. They had some kind of support from the outside. We always thought that it was Albania. They did have some support from Albania because they did transfer their open people across the border who were allegedly escaping, fleeing from the regime of Enver Hoxha. And then people kept silent about and they said well, all right, since they don't want this dictatorship of Enver Hoxha, let them come. And our state even bought property from the Serbs and gave them this land. However, when herds of cattle, horses, sheep were brought in, when they came with their families and when our television started showing this, that Albanian was moving en masse to Kosovo and Metohija, then we all started wondering what we would do? What would happen to us? And the terror was stepped up. That's how it all started.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I omitted to ask for these two exhibits only in relation to Mr. Bulatovic to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D294.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: D294 for both. Yes. Yes. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you resigned the Communist Party in 1967, and -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- because of Rankovic's removal in 1966? Was that the trigger?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... removing of Rankovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did I regard it. Rankovic was removed because he clashed with Tito and Kardelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was it then that led to your giving up the Communist Party in 1967?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, to leave it? Ah, I'll tell you all about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Briefly. In tab 2, when Rankovic was removed, then the leadership of the province including Fadil Hoxha thought that that was the right moment to replace all the top people in Kosovo and Metohija, who were Serbs at the time, to be removed from these high positions. Can you hear me, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They removed these people, and then they came across my manager where I worked as a worker. Dusan Samardzic from Gornja Dobrnja, he was the best manager, probably, in the entire Kosovo Export Company. He was in charge of crop production. When they dismissed him and when they forced him to retire, well, that was the case that led me to protest against that and that very evening, at that party meeting I left the party. I said that this party was pursuing a policy that was condemned and that I didn't want to be its member. Now, that's what is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From that moment onwards, were you concerned that the Serbs were being under-represented, underprotected in Kosovo? Was that your anxiety?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was persecution, people being removed from their positions and jobs. This kind of cleansing, ethnic cleansing, what they did on the 17th of March last year. That's the kind of action it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we move forward to the great constitutional changes of 1968 to 1971 embodied in the constitution of 1974. Were you one of those who found this constitution that didn't favour Serbs particularly offensive?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: One hundred per cent. That constitution was the root cause of all troubles, because then the Republic of Serbia was brought on a position of inequality in relation to the other Yugoslav republics. It was practically dismembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Judges have heard a lot about --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Like it or not, that constitution was brought in by the then legal government, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it gave Kosovo Albanians, because of their majority in the province, both power through representation and some expectations.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And from that moment on province both power through representation and some expectations.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And from that moment on, Serbs, including you, were dead set on reversing those constitutional changes; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I mean -- you may say and --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not interfere until the vandalism started. When they started vandalising cemeteries, killing Serbs. That is when I raised my voice. Before that, I did not engage in this thing. I'm not a lawyer, Mr. Nice, and it would have been silly for me to meddle in constitutional affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll just go back to the question. From that moment, that is from the 1974 constitution, there were Serbs who were dead set on reversing the constitutional changes. You subsequently associated yourself with that movement.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. There was no such movement. This is a lack of proper information. It's as if the previous provincial committee wrote it for you. This is false information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We come to the mid-1980s, passing over the demonstrations of 1981. I may came back to that next week; I may not. But would you accept, just in the most general terms, that there were any violations of the human rights of Kosovo Albanians in the course of the mid-1980s?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the Albanians? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Violation of the rights of Albanians? Was this done against the Albanians? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking whether you accept that. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: By who? Were they giving trouble to themselves? I mean, Mr. Nice, they were the majority. They had power in their hands. How could they act against themselves? This is a bit of a difficult question, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Rejecting that as a proposition and I'll come back to that if necessary next week.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now we can move very swiftly through the history because I don't challenge the account you give in general terms. We have your 1985 petition, your meeting with Ljubicic --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then we have the 1985 --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The October 1985 petition that we've seen. We haven't got it translated so we'll look at it next week. Then there was another petition and we've distributed it already -- I'm thinking it was the one that you were talking about. I'd ask you for a few comments on that. So if the Chamber's got that document, I'm not sure that I've got a version of this at the moment in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the one in the document The Destruction Of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I have a Serbian version of that. I'll make the Serbian version available to -- maybe he's got it. He's got it in his red book. Just look at this petition, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just look at this document, please. Have you got a document there in Serbian, Mr. Bulatovic, coming your way?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's not it. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here it comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Put that on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Cosic. This has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was -- well, Cosic was the man who advised you, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, to address the legal authorities and to write a petition, yes. But not what this gentleman brought here, no. Here's the petition right here. I have the text of the petition right here. And the text of the petition is supported by prominent public figures who supported it. October is my petition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure we're talking about the same petition, Mr. Bulatovic. Just follow what the Prosecutor is asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 1985 October petition we'll look at next week when we've found an English version of it or got it translated. That was followed by a January 1986 petition signed by a number of Belgrade intellectuals, and you'll be provided with a Serbian version of that.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Prendergast has got that --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The usher is going to hand you that. And on the overhead projector we're going to read a few passages of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd go to the next page, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is. It's right here the petition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This petition starts off by reference to the October 1985 petition, sets out in the second paragraph down that: "The petitioners were amazed and dejected by the authorities' reaction to this petition, by the threatening response by officials in Kosovo and by the attitude of the highest Serbian and all-Yugoslav authorities." Then, Mr. Bulatovic, if you go over two paragraphs and if we go to page numbered 50 at the top left-hand side --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Prendergast. You will see a paragraph that begins: "The political condemnation of the Petition has therefore moved us, the undersigned, to turn to public opinion with an appeal to support its demands for a radical change --"

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I have the Serbian version handed to -- made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you'll find it -- it's about five paragraphs down and the paragraph begins "The political condemnation."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But that's not it. That's not it. This is the petition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I'm not talking about your October 1985 petition. We're going to deal with that if at all when we've got it translated next week. I'm dealing with a different petition which is the one which was drafted by the intellectuals, signed by many of them, in January 1986, and it's this paragraph where --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I've got it right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you may find it helpful to follow it in the larger --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There we are. Now, at the end of the paragraph you're looking at, it says this, four lines up: "Only the protectors of the --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I receive a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It should be attached. It should be attached to the back of the English-language version that was distributed earlier. For the accused's assistance in the Serbian version on page 44 I think towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I read: "Only the protectors of the tyrants have changed. The Ottoman Empire, the Habsburg Monarchy, Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany have been replaced by the Albanian state and the ruling institutions of Kosovo. In place of forced Islamisation and Fascism there is Stalinised chauvinism. The only novelty is the fusion of tribal hatred and genocide masked by Marxism." These very strong expressions or views coming from the intellectuals, we may look at the signatures later, were these the expressions or views that you discussed with Cosic when he advised you on your petition?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these the sort of views that were current amongst those Serbs who had the interest to reverse constitutional change?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We, Mr. Nice, were in favour of constitutional changes that would bring us onto a footing of equality with all others -- and also in Metohija bring us onto a footing of equality with all others in Kosovo and Metohija and in Serbia. We did not work on any kind of text. We wrote our request, our petition, and it was attacked. Then these people supported our petition. They are well-known democrats from Serbia. They are not Stalinists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at the next paragraph to see the sort of material that was being broadcast or -- yes, distributed and broadcast, because I'm going to ask you about this, it creates the environment in which you and the accused came to operate. So we come to see in the next paragraph: "The methods have remained the same: The old poles now carry new heads. The new Deacon Avakum is called Djordje Martinovic, the new mother of the Jugoviches - Danica Milincic. Old women and nuns are raped, frail children" --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... this material, help us if I've got this right, Mr. Bulatovic, you would say this is an accurate contemporary description of life in Kosovo, or do you think this might have about it the whiff of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is correct. When he says here the blinding of cattle, that's true. They blinded a bull from the monastery of Devic. And when they were interrogating the young man who did this, he said I did that because the bull is a Serb bull. I think that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two more references from this document and then I'll be done it. The next paragraph but one says: "Under cover of the struggle against great-Serb hegemonism, a rigged political trial of the Serb nation and its history has been going on for decades. The first goal is an ethnically pure Kosovo, to be followed by further conquest of Serbian, Macedonian" --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- "and Montenegrin territories." Now, was this the prevailing belief of Serbs, that all Serbian territories were going to be attacked --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- by Albanians?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were really going to make your fellow Serbs believe that Albania was going to take over Serbia? Is that what was the prevailing thought?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Bulatovic has nothing to do with this petition. This petition was written by Serb intellectuals as it says here. It was written by academicians, professors, et cetera. He has nothing to do with that petition. He spoke of a petition that preceded this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, he had nothing to do with the writing of it, but Mr. Nice is addressing certain factual situations that are referred to and the witness can speak to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move on. But let me just make sure I've really understood the belief at the time being advanced and circulated, that the Albanians were going to take over Serbia, Macedonia, and Montenegro. Was that what you really all believed and were suggesting might happen?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But it happened, Mr. Nice. You helped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at the next paragraph that begins with the words "the absence of law," but we can go down to the end of this paragraph where we see yet -- I say yet another reference. We see a reference to the coke bottle case of Djordje Martinovic described as "a crime hard to find" -- "even among crimes it would be hard to find a crime like this." And if we go on, if you would be good enough, two more paragraphs we see: "Everyone in this country who is not indifferent has long ago realised that the genocide in Kosovo cannot be combatted without deep social and political changes in the whole country." Now, that's the material. We'll have to look at the translated version of your earlier petition when we get it by next Tuesday. What I'm going to suggest to you is this: That the environment into which you took this accused as a leader was an environment poisoned by propaganda. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. We did not call him as any kind of leader. We called him as the president of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia just like we called a year before that, a year before him, Ivan Stambolic. So don't -- don't call that any kind of leader. Don't. You're speaking in a highly tendentious way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In case there was a confusion in the translation of my question and the use of one particular word, let me rephrase the question in another way so that you can deal with it before if the Court so decides we break. By the time of the Kosovo Polje meetings and by the time of the events of the following year in which you and others were involved, there was a movement created by Serbs, including the intellectuals like Cosic, reflected in this sort of document that was poisoned by propaganda. That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. There was no movement that was created or was anyone ever elected any kind of leader or whatever. All the people were the leader. Everyone was guided by his own trouble and they expressed their troubles in public, and if what you are saying is what you are saying, let it be, but I disagree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll stop for the day. We'll resume tomorrow morning at -- we will resume on Tuesday. Tuesday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
